creatures.spottingTips: Look in rocky crevices and under boulders. Watch for a midden of shells outside their den. They change color to match surroundings perfectly.
creatures.description: The most iconic Mediterranean cephalopod — highly intelligent, capable of solving puzzles, using tools, and changing skin color and texture in milliseconds.
creatures.behavior: Solitary and territorial. Hunts crabs, bivalves, and fish. Collects shells and rocks to fortify den entrances.
funFacts: Has three hearts and blue blood
Each arm has independent neural control
Can squeeze through any opening larger than its beak

creatures.spottingTips: Often seen resting on rocky ledges or near underwater caves. Territorial but curious — it may approach divers. Look for its marbled brown and orange pattern.
creatures.description: One of the most charismatic fish in the Mediterranean. Once heavily fished, populations are recovering inside marine protected areas. Old males can live over 50 years.
creatures.behavior: Protogynous hermaphrodite — all start as females, and the dominant individual becomes male. Solitary and territorial.
funFacts: All groupers are born female; the dominant individual becomes male
Can live over 50 years
A keystone species of Mediterranean rocky reefs

creatures.spottingTips: Often seen at the surface breathing. Look near posidonia meadows where they feed. Approach slowly from the side — frontal approach spooks them.
creatures.description: The most common sea turtle in the Mediterranean, named for its large head and powerful jaw. Nests on beaches from Greece to Turkey and Spain.
creatures.behavior: Solitary, wide-ranging. Feeds on jellyfish, crustaceans, and mollusks. Nests on Mediterranean beaches May–August.
funFacts: Returns to the same beach where it hatched to nest decades later
Uses Earth's magnetic field for ocean navigation
Can hold its breath for up to 7 hours when resting

creatures.spottingTips: Extremely common on rocky Mediterranean shores. Found in dense clusters in intertidal and shallow rocky areas.
creatures.description: One of the most abundant echinoderms in the Mediterranean, playing a key ecological role as a grazer controlling algae growth on rocky reefs.
creatures.behavior: Gregarious, found in dense aggregations. Grazes on algae and seagrass. Can bore into soft rock to create shelter pits.
funFacts: Its gonads (roe) are a prized delicacy in Mediterranean cuisine
Can live up to 30 years
Overgrazing by urchins can create bare 'urchin barrens'

creatures.spottingTips: Often seen in large swarms near the surface in summer. CAUTION: extremely potent sting, even from tentacle fragments on the beach.
creatures.description: One of the most painful jellyfish in the Mediterranean. 'Noctiluca' means night light — it bioluminesces when disturbed at night.
creatures.behavior: Pelagic, moves with currents. Bioluminescent when disturbed. Forms massive blooms in warm months. Unlike most jellyfish, has no polyp stage.
funFacts: Bioluminesces with a blue-purple glow when disturbed at night
No polyp stage — it goes directly from egg to medusa
Its nematocysts remain active even when dead or stranded on a beach

creatures.spottingTips: Often patrolling rocky reefs in small groups. Look for their silver-grey torpedo shape near the reef edge. More active at dawn and dusk.
creatures.description: The European sea bass is one of the most prized fish in Mediterranean cuisine and sport fishing. A sleek, powerful predator of rocky coasts and open water.
creatures.behavior: Hunts in small groups, ambushing prey near structure. Enters estuaries and lagoons. Highly adaptable to varying salinity.
funFacts: One of the most farmed fish in Mediterranean aquaculture
Can enter freshwater rivers and estuaries
Juveniles form large schools for protection

creatures.spottingTips: Look for their head peering from crevices during the day. They constantly open and close their mouth — this is breathing, not aggression. Do not feed.
creatures.description: The moray eel is a powerful ambush predator of Mediterranean rocky reefs. Its marbled brown-yellow skin provides excellent camouflage in rocky crevices.
creatures.behavior: Largely nocturnal, hides in crevices by day. Has a second set of pharyngeal jaws to grip prey. Occasionally hunts cooperatively with groupers.
funFacts: Has two sets of jaws — a second pharyngeal jaw shoots forward to grip prey
Known to cooperate with groupers on hunting expeditions
Poor eyesight compensated by an excellent sense of smell

creatures.spottingTips: Almost impossible to spot at rest — it mimics a rock perfectly. Look for eyes and an unusual rock shape on the seafloor. Never touch rocky reef surfaces.
creatures.description: The master of camouflage on Mediterranean reefs. Sits motionless on the seafloor, virtually indistinguishable from surrounding rock, waiting to ambush passing prey.
creatures.behavior: Completely sedentary ambush predator. Relies entirely on camouflage. Lunges at prey with explosive speed. Dorsal spines deliver a painful venomous sting.
funFacts: Its dorsal spines are venomous and cause intense pain
Can lunge and swallow prey in 1/100th of a second
Periodically sheds its skin to remove algae fouling its camouflage

creatures.spottingTips: One of the most common colourful fish in the Med. Females are drab brown; males display vivid orange, green, and blue. Often seen darting over posidonia meadows.
creatures.description: The rainbow wrasse is among the most striking fish on Mediterranean reefs. Like all wrasses, females can transform into males as they grow larger.
creatures.behavior: Active by day, buries itself in sand at night. Females and juveniles form loose groups; males are territorial. Cleans parasites from other fish.
funFacts: Females can turn into males when needed — a process called protogynous hermaphroditism
Buries itself in sand to sleep at night
Acts as a cleaner fish, removing parasites from larger species

creatures.spottingTips: Unmissable — one of the most abundant fish on Mediterranean rocky reefs. Large schools hover above rocky outcrops. Juveniles are iridescent electric blue.
creatures.description: The damselfish is the most familiar fish of Mediterranean rocky reefs, forming large shimmering schools above rocky outcrops. Juveniles are brilliant iridescent blue.
creatures.behavior: Forms large schools above rocky reefs. Males guard nesting sites aggressively despite their tiny size. Feeds on plankton in the water column.
funFacts: Juveniles are brilliant metallic blue, fading to brown as adults
Males vigorously guard their egg patches from intruders much larger than themselves
One of the most abundant fish in the entire Mediterranean Sea

creatures.spottingTips: Extremely difficult to spot — masters of camouflage in posidonia. Look for their distinctive S-shaped silhouette clinging to seagrass stems. Move extremely slowly.
creatures.description: The long-snouted seahorse is one of two seahorse species in the Mediterranean. Anchors itself to seagrass with its prehensile tail.
creatures.behavior: Monogamous pairs meet daily to reinforce their bond. Males carry eggs in a brood pouch and give birth. Ambushes tiny crustaceans with a rapid head strike.
creatures.diet: Small crustaceans, mysid shrimp, tiny fish
funFacts: Males get pregnant and give birth — the female deposits eggs into the male's pouch
Cannot close their eyes — they have no eyelids
The slowest-moving fish in the sea, reaching only ~1.5m/hour

creatures.spottingTips: Moves very slowly and presents its thin profile head-on, making it near-invisible to prey. Look for the distinctive black bullseye spot on its flank.
creatures.description: The John Dory is a peculiar flat-bodied ambush predator. Its paper-thin profile makes it nearly invisible when facing head-on, allowing it to stalk prey undetected.
creatures.behavior: Stalks prey slowly head-on, then strikes with an extendable jaw. The large black spot on its flank is thought to startle predators.
funFacts: Its extensible jaw can shoot forward to capture prey
The black spot on its side is said to be St. Peter's thumbprint (hence 'Saint Pierre' in French)
Its paper-thin profile makes it nearly invisible head-on

creatures.spottingTips: Look for small groups foraging along the seafloor, using their barbels to probe sand. Bright red-orange colouration makes them easy to spot against sandy bottoms.
creatures.description: The striped red mullet is one of the most colourful and prized table fish in the Mediterranean, often seen probing the seafloor with its sensitive chin barbels.
creatures.behavior: Forages in groups, using twin chin barbels to detect invertebrates buried in sand or under rocks.
funFacts: The chin barbels are packed with taste receptors for finding buried prey
Highly prized in Mediterranean cuisine since ancient Roman times
Can rapidly change colour intensity when excited

creatures.spottingTips: Rare and fast — occasionally seen in blue water when diving offshore. Look for fast-moving blue-silver torpedo shapes. Often accompanied by feeding seabirds at the surface.
creatures.description: The Atlantic bluefin tuna is the largest tuna species and one of the ocean's most powerful predators. It can maintain body temperature above ambient — a rare trait among fish.
creatures.behavior: Highly migratory, crossing the Atlantic annually. Enters the Mediterranean to spawn in summer. Reaches speeds of 70 km/h.
funFacts: Can maintain body temperature above ambient water — a rare ability among fish
Reaches speeds of over 70 km/h
A single large individual can fetch over $1 million at auction in Japan

creatures.spottingTips: Often seen in tight cylindrical schools hovering in open water near reef drop-offs. Look for their long silver torpedo shapes and underbite jaw.
creatures.description: The European barracuda forms spectacular schooling tornadoes in the Mediterranean, especially around underwater pinnacles and reef walls.
creatures.behavior: Juveniles and sub-adults school in tight formations. Adults become solitary. Notorious for being attracted to shiny objects.
funFacts: Juveniles form spectacular cylindrical tornado schools called 'bait balls'
Attracted to shiny objects — remove dangling jewellery before diving
Can accelerate from 0 to full speed almost instantly

creatures.spottingTips: Look on sandy or muddy bottoms at night. Rests motionless on the seafloor during the day wedged under rocks. Spotted pattern distinguishes it from other small sharks.
creatures.description: The most common shark in the Mediterranean, the catshark is a small, harmless bottom-dweller with a beautiful spotted pattern. Its egg cases — 'mermaid's purses' — wash up on beaches.
creatures.behavior: Nocturnal bottom-dweller. Lays rectangular egg cases anchored to seabed structure. Congregates in male or female groups.
funFacts: Its egg cases are called 'mermaid's purses' and often wash up on beaches
Can detect electrical fields from hidden prey using ampullae of Lorenzini
Completely harmless to humans

creatures.spottingTips: Offshore pelagic species, rarely encountered by recreational divers. Best spotted on blue-water dives far offshore. Their vivid indigo-blue upper body is unmistakeable.
creatures.description: The blue shark is one of the most wide-ranging sharks in the world, with striking indigo-blue colouring. It occurs in the open Mediterranean but is rarely seen.
creatures.behavior: Highly migratory oceanic species. Often approaches boats slowly and curiously. Hunts schooling fish and squid near the surface at night.
funFacts: Can travel over 9,000 km in a single migration
Has an internal heat-exchange system to keep its brain and eyes warm
Among the most heavily fished sharks in the world

creatures.spottingTips: Rests partially buried in sand during the day. Look for a circular flat shape on sandy bottoms. NEVER touch — it can deliver a powerful electric shock.
creatures.description: The torpedo ray can discharge up to 200 volts of electricity to stun prey and deter predators. It lies buried in sand awaiting unsuspecting fish to swim overhead.
creatures.behavior: Buries in sand by day. Produces powerful electric discharges to immobilise prey. Ambushes fish from below.
funFacts: Can deliver an electric shock of up to 200 volts
The electric organ accounts for nearly a sixth of its body weight
Ancient Romans used torpedo rays to treat headaches and gout

creatures.spottingTips: Often buried just below the sand surface with only eyes and tail visible. Shuffle your feet when wading to warn rays and avoid stepping on them.
creatures.description: The common stingray glides gracefully over sandy Mediterranean bottoms, often burying itself in sand. Its tail carries a barbed venomous spine used only in defence.
creatures.behavior: Spends much of the day buried in sand. Flaps its pectoral fins to uncover buried prey. Uses the venomous tail spine defensively when stepped on.
funFacts: The tail spine is barbed and delivers venom — extremely painful but rarely fatal
Pectoral wings undulate in a wave pattern unlike sharks that beat a tail
Electroreceptors can detect a buried fish's heartbeat

creatures.spottingTips: Often seen gliding gracefully in open water above sandy bottoms. Their distinctive flat diamond shape and long whip tail are unmistakeable. Sometimes leaps out of the water.
creatures.description: The eagle ray soars through the water column on pointed triangular wings, diving to sandy bottoms to crush mollusks and crustaceans with its powerful plate-like teeth.
creatures.behavior: Highly mobile, cruises in open water. Occasionally forms aggregations. Known to leap completely out of the water.
funFacts: Plate-like teeth can crush the shells of thick clams effortlessly
Known to leap completely out of the water — possibly to dislodge parasites
Can swim long distances between feeding grounds

creatures.spottingTips: Look in shallow water over sandy or rocky bottoms. They hover with an undulating fin fringe and can shift through a mesmerising variety of patterns and colours.
creatures.description: The cuttlefish is arguably the most intelligent invertebrate in the sea, capable of sophisticated communication through its skin colour and texture. Its internal cuttlebone provides buoyancy.
creatures.behavior: Solitary hunter. Hypnotises prey with rippling colour patterns before striking with lightning speed. Males perform elaborate colour displays to compete for females.
funFacts: Has the highest brain-to-body ratio of any invertebrate
Has W-shaped pupils that give them nearly 360° vision
Uses polarised light patterns — invisible to humans — in skin displays

creatures.spottingTips: Most active at night when they rise toward the surface. Attracted to dive lights. Look for torpedo-shaped silvery shapes in open water. They often hover in mid-water.
creatures.description: The European squid is the most commercially important cephalopod in the Mediterranean, forming large schools and aggregating to spawn on sandy bottoms.
creatures.behavior: Forms large schools. Males compete for females with colour displays. Aggregates on sandy bottoms to lay clusters of egg cases. Rises to surface at night.
funFacts: Can jet backwards at high speed using siphon propulsion
Ink is edible and used in Mediterranean cooking (squid ink pasta)
Spawning aggregations can involve thousands of individuals

creatures.spottingTips: Smaller and less common than the common octopus. Distinguished by a single row of suckers on each arm (common octopus has two). Emits a strong musky odour when handled.
creatures.description: The musky octopus is the common octopus's smaller cousin, identifiable by a single row of suckers per arm and a distinctive musky smell. Found from shallow reefs to bathyal depths.
creatures.behavior: Solitary and nocturnal. More common in deeper water than O. vulgaris. Emits strong musk odour as a defence mechanism.
funFacts: Has only one row of suckers per arm, unlike the two rows of the common octopus
Emits a strong musky smell — its Latin name 'cirrhosa' refers to its curled arm tips
Can be found as deep as 500m

creatures.spottingTips: Hides in rocky crevices and cave entrances by day with only antennae visible. Look for long orange antennae protruding from dark gaps. Very wary — approach slowly.
creatures.description: The spiny lobster is the prized jewel of Mediterranean fishing. Lacks the large claws of Atlantic lobsters but makes up for it with magnificent long spiny antennae.
creatures.behavior: Nocturnal forager. Shelters in rocky crevices by day. Makes mass migrations along the seafloor in autumn, forming queues of hundreds walking in single file.
funFacts: Makes epic single-file migrations of hundreds of individuals in autumn
Has no large claws — uses stridulation (rubbing antennae) to produce warning sounds
Can live over 20 years and grow to 5kg

creatures.spottingTips: Often seen in posidonia meadows or rocky shallows. Can aggregate in huge moulting piles in spring. Its spiny red-orange carapace decorated with algae and sponges for camouflage.
creatures.description: The spiny spider crab is the largest crab in the Mediterranean, famous for its extraordinary moulting aggregations of thousands of individuals in spring.
creatures.behavior: Decorates its shell with algae and sponge fragments for camouflage. Aggregates in huge clusters of thousands for moulting in spring.
funFacts: Aggregates in piles of thousands to moult — one of the Mediterranean's most spectacular wildlife events
Actively decorates its carapace with sponge and algae for camouflage
A prized delicacy — known as 'granceola' in Venice

creatures.spottingTips: Look for U-shaped burrow openings in sandy or muddy bottoms. Rarely leaves its burrow. Peer into burrow entrances carefully — but do not put fingers in!
creatures.description: Despite its delicate appearance, the mantis shrimp has one of the fastest and most powerful strikes in the animal kingdom, capable of shattering glass aquarium walls.
creatures.behavior: Lives in U-shaped burrows in sandy-muddy sediment. Strikes prey with explosive 'smasher' appendages. Has the most complex eyes of any animal, seeing 16 colour channels.
funFacts: Its strike accelerates at 10,400 g — one of the fastest movements in the animal kingdom
Has 16 types of colour-receptor cells (humans have 3)
The force of its strike can shatter aquarium glass

creatures.spottingTips: Rarely seen due to intense fishing pressure — now critically rare outside protected areas. If spotted, it will be in a deep rocky crevice or cave. Look for its broad flat antennae.
creatures.description: The slipper lobster is a massive, flat-bodied crustacean with plate-like flattened antennae. Once common, it has been nearly wiped out by fishing outside protected areas.
creatures.behavior: Nocturnal, hides in rocky crevices and caves by day. Moves along the reef at night foraging for mollusks. Extremely long-lived.
funFacts: One of the most heavily depleted species in the Mediterranean — now a rarity
Its flattened antennae are called 'scaphocerites' and are unique among lobsters
Can live over 15 years and weigh up to 4kg

creatures.spottingTips: Stands vertically in posidonia meadows with only the pointed base buried in sand. Its fan-shaped shell can reach 120cm. Now critically rare — a sighting is very special.
creatures.description: The noble pen shell is the largest bivalve in the Mediterranean and critically endangered following a mass mortality event from a parasite that has wiped out over 99% of the population.
creatures.behavior: Sessile filter feeder anchored in posidonia meadows. Harbours a commensal shrimp-crab pair inside its mantle. Secretes fine 'sea silk' (byssus threads).
funFacts: Critically endangered — over 99% of the population died from a parasite in 2016–2019
Produces 'sea silk' (byssus) — once woven into garments for Mediterranean royalty
The largest bivalve in the Mediterranean, reaching over 1 metre

creatures.spottingTips: Forms dense colonies on any hard substrate in the intertidal zone. The blue-black shells are unmistakeable. One of the most abundant organisms on Mediterranean rocky shores.
creatures.description: The Mediterranean mussel forms dense colonies on wave-exposed rocky shores, creating an important habitat for dozens of associated species. A cornerstone of Mediterranean seafood.
creatures.behavior: Sessile filter feeder. Attaches to rock with strong byssus threads. Forms mussel beds that provide shelter for other invertebrates.
funFacts: Can filter up to 3 litres of water per hour
Byssus threads are used in research to develop ultra-strong waterproof adhesives
One of the most farmed shellfish in the world

creatures.spottingTips: Look on sandy bottoms — often partially buried. When threatened, can jet-propel itself by clapping its shell halves. Has up to 200 primitive eyes along its mantle edge.
creatures.description: The Mediterranean scallop has up to 200 tiny blue eyes along its mantle — each with a lens, retina, and cornea. Its fan-shaped shell has been a symbol of pilgrimage for centuries.
creatures.behavior: Rests on sandy or muddy bottoms. Claps shell halves rapidly to swim away from predators. Has numerous primitive eyes detecting light and shadow.
funFacts: Has up to 200 simple eyes arranged along its mantle edge
Can swim by clapping its shell valves to escape starfish
The pilgrim's shell of the Camino de Santiago is based on this species

creatures.spottingTips: Look in shallow rocky areas and on boulders. Its spiny shell with banded markings is distinctive. Often found in groups on rocky substrates at low tide.
creatures.description: The banded murex was the source of Tyrian purple, the most expensive dye in the ancient world used for imperial Roman robes. Its secretion was extracted to produce the precious pigment.
creatures.behavior: Predatory gastropod that drills holes through bivalve shells to extract the contents. Lays vase-shaped egg capsules on rocky surfaces.
funFacts: Source of Tyrian purple dye — the most expensive pigment in the ancient world
It takes 12,000 murex snails to produce 1.4g of purple dye
The dye was reserved for emperors and high priests in antiquity

creatures.spottingTips: Completely concealed inside limestone rock — you'll see only a small hole. Never break open rock to find them: it is strictly illegal throughout the Mediterranean.
creatures.description: The date mussel lives completely encased in rock, slowly boring into limestone over decades. Critically protected — harvesting requires destroying the rock and is illegal across the Mediterranean.
creatures.behavior: Bores into limestone using acid secretions and shell-rocking abrasion. Lives up to 30+ years inside its rock chamber. Filter feeds through siphons extended into the water.
funFacts: Lives its entire adult life cemented inside a self-bored limestone chamber
Takes decades to bore just a few centimetres into rock
Illegal to harvest throughout the Mediterranean — populations are severely depleted

creatures.spottingTips: One of the most common and striking animals on Mediterranean rocky reefs. Its bright red colour makes it easy to spot against dark rock. Often seen on vertical walls.
creatures.description: The red starfish is one of the most recognisable symbols of Mediterranean reef diving — a vivid red star that contrasts brilliantly against dark rocky walls.
creatures.behavior: Slow-moving predator. Pushes its stomach out of its body to digest prey externally. Can regenerate lost arms. Moves using hundreds of tiny tube feet.
funFacts: Pushes its entire stomach outside its body to digest prey
Can regenerate a complete new body from a single arm
Has no blood — uses filtered seawater in its vascular system

creatures.spottingTips: Look on rocky walls and ledges in current-swept areas. Spreads its feathery arms to catch plankton drifting by. Can be red, orange, yellow, or white.
creatures.description: The feather star is the most ancient class of echinoderms, unchanged for 480 million years. It perches on rocky outcrops and fans its feathery arms in the current to catch drifting plankton.
creatures.behavior: Clings to rock with hooked cirri. Fans pinnulate arms in currents to catch plankton. Can swim slowly by waving arms. Moves to shaded spots when light is bright.
funFacts: An ancient design unchanged for 480 million years
Can swim by coordinating arm movements like a butterfly stroke
The feathery arms are called 'pinnules' and are covered in sticky tube feet

creatures.spottingTips: Very common on rocky and sandy Mediterranean bottoms. Often seen slowly moving or motionless. Don't disturb — when threatened it ejects its internal organs (evisceration).
creatures.description: The sea cucumber plays a vital role as a sediment detoxifier, ingesting sand and sediment and recycling nutrients. It can expel its internal organs as a defence mechanism.
creatures.behavior: Slow-moving detritus feeder. When severely threatened, eviserates — expelling internal organs (which regenerate) to entangle predators. Some species expel sticky Cuvierian tubules.
creatures.diet: Detritus, bacteria, organic particles in sediment
funFacts: When threatened, can eject its internal organs — which fully regenerate afterwards
Processes enormous quantities of sediment, recycling nutrients like an underwater earthworm
Can liquefy and reform its body to squeeze through crevices

creatures.spottingTips: Hides under rocks and in crevices by day. Turn over a rock gently and you may find several. Fast-moving — arms writhe rapidly when disturbed. Nocturnal forager.
creatures.description: The brittle star moves with astonishing agility for an echinoderm, its five long flexible arms writhing snake-like across the seafloor. Often hides under rocks and in posidonia.
creatures.behavior: Nocturnal forager. Hides under rocks by day. Moves arms in a rowing motion to escape quickly. Arms break off easily as a defence (autotomy) and regrow.
funFacts: Arms break off voluntarily as a defence and grow back completely
One of the fastest-moving echinoderms — moves its arms in a rowing motion
Aggregates in huge numbers under boulders in sheltered areas

creatures.spottingTips: Found on exposed rocky surfaces, often in areas with less algae than purple urchins. Uniformly black with shorter spines than Paracentrotus. Avoid touching — spines break off in skin.
creatures.description: The black sea urchin is a grazer of exposed rocky surfaces, favouring wave-exposed areas. Its uniform jet-black colour and shorter spines distinguish it from the purple sea urchin.
creatures.behavior: Grazes on encrusting algae and coralline algae on rocky surfaces. Prefers more exposed, wave-battered sites than the purple urchin.
funFacts: Spines break off in skin and are difficult to remove — they dissolve over several weeks
Does not eat posidonia or macro-algae like the purple urchin — a specialist grazer
Thrives in areas where algae coverage would otherwise be dense

creatures.spottingTips: Rarer than the loggerhead in the Mediterranean. Often seen grazing in posidonia meadows — look for slow, deliberate munching movements. Named for the green colour of its fat, not its shell.
creatures.description: The green sea turtle is rarer in the Mediterranean than the loggerhead, primarily a herbivore that grazes on posidonia seagrass and algae. Named for the green colour of its fat.
creatures.behavior: The only fully herbivorous sea turtle as an adult. Grazes on seagrass and algae. Nests primarily in Cyprus and Turkey in the Mediterranean.
funFacts: Named for the green colour of its fat, not its shell
The only fully herbivorous sea turtle as an adult
Main Mediterranean nesting beach is Alagadi in Cyprus

creatures.spottingTips: Often approaches boats to bow-ride. Look for dorsal fins breaking the surface. Individual dolphins can be identified by notches and scars on their dorsal fins.
creatures.description: The bottlenose dolphin is the most common cetacean in the Mediterranean — intelligent, social, and curious. Resident groups live in coastal waters year-round.
creatures.behavior: Lives in social groups of 2–15. Uses echolocation to hunt fish. Known to cooperate with fishermen, herding fish toward nets in exchange for scraps.
funFacts: Uses signature whistles — essentially unique names — to call each other
Sleeps with one brain hemisphere at a time to remain alert
Individual dolphins are identified by the unique shape of their dorsal fin

creatures.spottingTips: Often seen in large groups of 10–500 in offshore blue water. Famous for spectacular acrobatic leaps. The distinctive blue and white stripe pattern is unmistakeable.
creatures.description: The striped dolphin is the most abundant cetacean in the Mediterranean — spectacular offshore herds of hundreds can be seen, performing acrobatic leaps.
creatures.behavior: Highly acrobatic — performs 'roto-tailing' leaps up to 7m high. Lives in large offshore groups. Dives to 700m to hunt deep-water squid.
funFacts: Famous for 'roto-tailing' — spinning somersaults up to 7 metres above the surface
Mediterranean population (around 90,000) is the largest in the world
Dives up to 700m to hunt deep-water squid

creatures.spottingTips: With only ~800 individuals remaining, an encounter is exceptionally rare. Rests in isolated sea caves. Observe from a great distance — any disturbance can cause pups to be abandoned.
creatures.description: The Mediterranean monk seal is one of the rarest marine mammals on Earth, with fewer than 800 individuals surviving. Any sighting should be reported to conservation authorities.
creatures.behavior: Extremely shy and sensitive to human disturbance. Rests and pups in isolated sea caves. Forages over large areas along rocky coasts.
funFacts: One of the rarest marine mammals on Earth — fewer than 800 individuals remain
Pups are born with black woolly fur that moults to adult colouration
Ancient Greeks and Romans considered it sacred to both Poseidon and Apollo

creatures.spottingTips: Seen offshore in deep water areas (>1000m). Breaths are bushy and projected forward at 45°. Tail flukes raised vertically before a deep dive. The Ligurian-Provençal basin is a hotspot.
creatures.description: The sperm whale is the largest toothed predator on Earth and a regular visitor to the deep canyons of the western Mediterranean. It dives to 3,000m hunting giant squid.
creatures.behavior: Dives to over 3,000m for up to 90 minutes. Produces the loudest sounds of any animal. Social groups of females and calves; males solitary.
funFacts: Produces the loudest sounds of any animal — clicks at over 230 dB
Has the largest brain of any animal to have ever lived
The Pelagos Sanctuary in the Ligurian Sea is a major Mediterranean habitat

creatures.spottingTips: Blow can reach 6–8m high and is visible from far away. The Ligurian Sea and Strait of Sicily are hotspots in summer. Dorsal fin appears after the blow, well behind the head.
creatures.description: The second-largest animal on Earth visits the western Mediterranean every summer to feed on krill. The Ligurian Sea hosts a resident feeding aggregation.
creatures.behavior: Filter feeds on krill and small fish by lunge-feeding. The Ligurian-Provençal Basin supports a summer feeding aggregation of around 500 individuals.
funFacts: The second-largest animal ever to have lived on Earth
The Pelagos Sanctuary in the Ligurian Sea protects ~500 Mediterranean fin whales
Asymmetrically coloured — white lower jaw on right, dark on left, possibly for confusing prey

creatures.spottingTips: One of the most common jellyfish worldwide. Forms huge surface blooms in spring and summer. Nearly transparent with four distinctive purple-pink rings (gonads) visible through the bell.
creatures.description: The moon jellyfish is one of the most recognisable jellyfish in the world — translucent white with four pink-purple rings. Its sting is mild and rarely affects humans.
creatures.behavior: Largely passive drifter, moved by currents. Forms dense blooms. Can survive in very low-oxygen water. Polyp stage on the seafloor alternates with medusa stage.
funFacts: Has been sent to space — NASA studied its adaptation to zero-gravity
Sting is mild and not dangerous to humans
Can survive in waters with almost no oxygen

creatures.spottingTips: Hard to miss — one of the largest jellyfish in the Mediterranean. White dome bell with purple frilly oral arms below. Harmless to most people. Often has small fish sheltering inside.
creatures.description: The barrel jellyfish is the largest jellyfish in the Mediterranean, reaching 90cm across. Its enormous frilled oral arms filter plankton. Small fish and crabs often shelter inside its bell.
creatures.behavior: Slow drifter, pulsing bell weakly. Harbours commensal juvenile fish (horse mackerel) and crabs under its bell. No true tentacles — feeding occurs through oral arms.
funFacts: Can weigh over 35kg — the largest jellyfish in the Mediterranean
Small fish and crabs shelter inside its bell as protection
Leatherback turtles migrate to the Mediterranean specifically to eat barrel jellyfish

creatures.spottingTips: Unmistakeable — a yellow domed bell with a raised yellow centre, resembling a fried egg. Harmless to humans. Forms blooms in late summer in the western Mediterranean.
creatures.description: The fried egg jellyfish looks exactly like a sunny-side-up egg drifting in the water. Its unusual yellow dome with raised central button makes it one of the most distinctive jellyfish in the Mediterranean.
creatures.behavior: Drifts with currents and weak pulsing. Entirely harmless to humans. Often has small juvenile fish sheltering among its short tentacles.
funFacts: Looks exactly like a fried egg floating in the sea
Hosts symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae) in its tissues for extra nutrition
Completely harmless to touch

creatures.spottingTips: DANGER — do not touch. Iridescent blue-purple float visible at the surface. Tentacles can trail up to 50m below. Even beached specimens retain active stinging cells.
creatures.description: The Portuguese man o'war is not a single animal but a colony of specialised organisms (zooids). Its sting is extremely painful and can cause serious medical emergencies.
creatures.behavior: Carried by wind using its gas-filled float as a sail. Stinging tentacles trail up to 50m below. Occasionally blown into the Mediterranean from the Atlantic.
funFacts: Not a jellyfish — it is a colony of four different types of specialised organism (zooids)
Tentacles can trail up to 50 metres below the surface
Its float acts as a sail — it cannot move independently but is steered by the wind

creatures.spottingTips: Look on shaded overhanging rock faces and cave ceilings below 20m. The red branching colony contrasts vividly with white open polyps when feeding. Now rare outside protected areas.
creatures.description: Mediterranean red coral has been harvested for jewellery since ancient times. It is legally protected throughout the Mediterranean but still threatened by illegal harvesting and climate warming.
creatures.behavior: Sessile colony of polyps feeding on plankton. Grows extremely slowly — 1–2cm per year. Polyps retract when disturbed.
funFacts: Grows only 1–2cm per year — a large colony may be over 100 years old
Has been harvested for jewellery since at least 25,000 years ago
Strictly protected — illegal to collect without authorisation throughout the EU

creatures.spottingTips: Fan-shaped yellow colonies attached to rocky walls and overhangs below 15m. Spreads perpendicular to current to maximise food capture. Often smothered with tiny reddish polyps when feeding.
creatures.description: The yellow gorgonian builds fan-shaped colonies on rocky walls, perpendicular to the current. Thousands of tiny polyps extend their tentacles into the flow to capture plankton.
creatures.behavior: Sessile colony. Fan shape spreads perpendicular to prevailing current for maximum plankton interception. Slow growing, sensitive to warming events.
funFacts: Mass mortality events during marine heat waves kill thousands of colonies simultaneously
Each branch supports hundreds of individual polyps
Its skeleton is made of a flexible protein called gorgonin

creatures.spottingTips: Extremely common in rock pools and shallow intertidal zones. At low tide retracts into a blob of jelly. Underwater, up to 192 tentacles spread out into a stunning flower shape.
creatures.description: The beadlet anemone is one of the most abundant animals on Mediterranean rocky shores, living in the intertidal zone and visible even without snorkelling equipment.
creatures.behavior: Retracts into a smooth blob when exposed to air at low tide. Stings other anemones that invade its territory using specialised tentacles called acontia.
funFacts: Can live for 80+ years — exceptionally long for such a small animal
Stings rival anemones that encroach on its territory
Has no skeleton — entirely soft-bodied, anchored to rock by its muscular base

creatures.spottingTips: Looks like a dark irregular lump or dome on rocky surfaces. Often colonised by other organisms — worms, mollusks, brittle stars. Squeeze gently to confirm it is a sponge.
creatures.description: The bath sponge is the ancestor of all natural bath sponges used since antiquity. Its flexible skeleton has no cells with a nucleus — it is among the most primitive multicellular animals.
creatures.behavior: Sessile filter feeder. Pumps thousands of litres of water per day through its body. Can regenerate from tiny fragments.
funFacts: Pumps 20,000 times its body volume of water through itself every day
Has been harvested in the Mediterranean for over 3,000 years as a cleaning tool
No true tissues or organs — the simplest multicellular animals alive today

creatures.spottingTips: Distinctive erect orange-yellow fingers or branching tree-like colonies on rocky walls below 15m. One of the most beautiful sponges on Mediterranean reefs.
creatures.description: The axinella sponge forms spectacular erect orange-yellow branching colonies on rocky Mediterranean walls. A key structural species providing shelter for dozens of invertebrates.
creatures.behavior: Sessile filter feeder. Upright columnar or branching growth maximises water flow through the sponge body.
funFacts: Contains bioactive compounds under research for potential anti-cancer applications
Provides crucial microhabitat for brittle stars, worms, and crustaceans
Can survive complete tissue loss and regenerate from the bare skeleton

creatures.spottingTips: Forms vast underwater meadows visible from above the surface in clear water. Look for dense ribbons of ribbon-like green leaves up to 1m long in sunlit shallow water.
creatures.description: Posidonia oceanica is the foundation species of Mediterranean coastal ecosystems — an endemic seagrass that forms vast meadows, produces oxygen, and supports thousands of species.
creatures.behavior: Grows slowly — about 1–7cm per year. Meadows can be thousands of years old. Dead leaves accumulate as 'banquettes' on beaches in autumn.
funFacts: Produces up to 20 litres of oxygen per day per square metre
One meadow clone off Ibiza is estimated to be up to 200,000 years old
Is endemic to the Mediterranean Sea — found nowhere else on Earth

creatures.spottingTips: Impossible to miss on any rocky Mediterranean shore in spring and summer. Bright translucent green sheets attached to rock in the intertidal zone. Can be collected and eaten.
creatures.description: Sea lettuce is the most familiar green alga on Mediterranean rocky shores — its vivid translucent green sheets are anchored to intertidal rocks and are edible, with a salty oceanic flavour.
creatures.behavior: Sessile, photosynthetic alga attached to rock. Forms green mats in spring. Can go adrift and form floating green carpets in calm bays if nutrients are high (eutrophication indicator).
funFacts: Edible — used in Japanese cuisine as 'aosa' and increasingly in Mediterranean cooking
When it forms dense floating mats, it indicates coastal nutrient pollution
Only two cells thick — one of the thinnest multicellular organisms

creatures.spottingTips: Look for small fan-shaped or funnel-shaped fronds with distinctive concentric white and brown stripes attached to shallow rocks. Often encrusted with white calcium carbonate.
creatures.description: The peacock's tail alga is one of the few brown algae to calcify its fronds, producing elegant fan-shaped thalli with distinctive concentric white rings visible on shallow rocky reefs.
creatures.behavior: Sessile photosynthetic alga. Deposits calcium carbonate in its fronds — one of the few brown algae to do so.
funFacts: One of the very few brown algae that deposits calcium carbonate in its fronds
The white rings are zones of calcification that alternate with non-calcified zones
Very sensitive to water quality — a good indicator of clean coastal water

creatures.spottingTips: Forms dense green carpets smothering the seafloor. Cylindrical fronds 2–3mm wide distinguish it from native algae. Do NOT cut or collect — fragments spread the infestation.
creatures.description: Caulerpa cylindracea is an invasive alga from Australia that has colonised most of the Mediterranean seafloor, smothering native seagrass and rocky reef communities.
creatures.behavior: Spreads rapidly via stolons and fragments. Releases toxins that inhibit native species. Can smother posidonia meadows and rocky reef communities. Nearly impossible to eradicate once established.
funFacts: Accidentally introduced to the Mediterranean from an aquarium in Monaco in the 1980s
Now covers thousands of square kilometres of Mediterranean seafloor
Do NOT cut it — each fragment can start a new infestation

creatures.spottingTips: Recognisable by the golden band between the eyes and a dark shoulder spot. Often seen alone or in small groups over posidonia meadows and sandy bottoms.
creatures.description: The gilt-head bream is one of the most prized fish in Mediterranean aquaculture and fishing. Its golden forehead band makes it instantly recognisable.
creatures.behavior: Solitary or in small groups. Crushes hard-shelled prey with powerful molar-like teeth. Moves between inshore breeding grounds and deeper winter habitat.
funFacts: Named for the distinctive gold stripe between its eyes
Its powerful crushing teeth can open thick mussel shells with ease
One of the most widely farmed fish in the Mediterranean

creatures.spottingTips: One of the most abundant reef fish in the Med. Look for silvery bodies with vertical dark bands and a black caudal spot. Usually in groups over rocky reefs.
creatures.description: The white seabream is among the most familiar fish on Mediterranean rocky reefs — gregarious, bold, and often curiously approaching divers.
creatures.behavior: Omnivorous and adaptable. Forms mixed schools with other seabream species. Juveniles in rock pools; adults move deeper with age.
funFacts: Juveniles inhabit rock pools, adults deeper reefs
Can hybridise with other Diplodus species
One of the most common fish on Mediterranean rocky reefs

creatures.spottingTips: Identified by two black bands: one at the base of the tail and one on the nape. Extremely common; forms large schools above rocky reefs.
creatures.description: One of the commonest fish throughout the Mediterranean, distinguished by its two bold black bands — one behind the head, one at the tail base.
creatures.behavior: Very gregarious — forms large mixed schools. Feeds on invertebrates by day. Protogynous hermaphrodite.
funFacts: The two black bands are unique to this species among Mediterranean seabreams
Juveniles often shelter in posidonia meadows
One of the most numerous fish in the Mediterranean Sea

creatures.spottingTips: One of the most common small predators on Mediterranean reefs. Its orange-brown stripes and alert posture make it easy to identify. Often perches on rock surfaces.
creatures.description: The comber is one of the most abundant small predators on Mediterranean reefs. A simultaneous hermaphrodite — every individual produces both eggs and sperm at the same time.
creatures.behavior: Perches on rocks watching for prey. Simultaneous hermaphrodite — individuals mate in pairs and both contribute eggs and sperm simultaneously.
funFacts: A simultaneous hermaphrodite — both male and female at the same time
Can fertilise its own eggs — a rare capability in vertebrates
One of the most abundant predatory fish on shallow Mediterranean reefs

creatures.spottingTips: More colourful than the comber — look for the striking blue and orange belly and the irregular dark body markings resembling Arabic script.
creatures.description: The painted comber is one of the most colourful small fish on Mediterranean rocky reefs, decorated with swirling lines said to resemble Arabic writing.
creatures.behavior: Solitary and territorial. Perches prominently on rocky outcrops. Simultaneous hermaphrodite like other combers.
funFacts: Its species name 'scriba' means 'scribe' — for its script-like flank markings
Has a vivid blue and violet belly patch unlike any other Mediterranean serranid
Also a simultaneous hermaphrodite

creatures.spottingTips: Dense silver schools in open water above rocky drop-offs. A line of bony scutes along the tail is diagnostic.
creatures.description: The horse mackerel forms massive shoals throughout the Mediterranean. An important prey species for tuna, dolphins, and seabirds.
creatures.behavior: Highly migratory schooling species. Forms mixed schools with other jacks and mackerels.
funFacts: Has a line of bony scutes along its lateral line — unique among Mediterranean jacks
Schools can contain millions of individuals
An important commercial fish throughout the Mediterranean

creatures.spottingTips: Enormous shimmering schools near the surface especially in spring and autumn. A row of dark spots runs along the upper flank.
creatures.description: The European pilchard forms vast shoals that feed nearly every larger predator in the Mediterranean — a true cornerstone of the ecosystem.
creatures.behavior: Forms gigantic schools. Rises toward the surface at night to feed on plankton. Crucial link between plankton and higher predators.
funFacts: A sardine is simply a young or small European pilchard
One of the most important forage fish in the Mediterranean ecosystem
Schools attract dolphins, tuna, and seabirds simultaneously

creatures.spottingTips: Dense flashing schools near the surface especially at dusk. Recognisable by the protruding snout and large mouth extending behind the eye.
creatures.description: The European anchovy is a keystone species of the Mediterranean ecosystem — its vast schools feed dolphins, tuna, swordfish, and seabirds alike.
creatures.behavior: Highly schooling. Forms bait balls when under attack. Undertakes seasonal migrations across the Mediterranean.
funFacts: Fermented anchovy paste was the ancient Romans' favourite condiment ('garum')
Schools form tight bait balls when attacked by dolphins and tuna simultaneously
One of the most commercially important fish in the Mediterranean

creatures.spottingTips: Hides in rocky crevices and caves by day with its large flat head visible. Much larger than a moray — can reach 3m. Adults are generally docile unless cornered.
creatures.description: The European conger is the world's largest eel, reaching 3 metres and 110kg. It hides in rocky crevices by day and hunts at night across the entire Mediterranean.
creatures.behavior: Sedentary by day, active hunter at night. Spawns once in deep Atlantic water, then dies. Juveniles migrate back to the Mediterranean.
funFacts: The world's largest eel — can reach 3 metres and over 100kg
Spawns once in its lifetime deep in the Atlantic, then dies
Females are twice the size of males

creatures.spottingTips: Skims the surface in loose schools, its long silver-green body visible just below the water. Often leaps when startled. Best spotted while snorkelling near the surface.
creatures.description: The garfish is a surface-living predator named for its elongated beak. Its bones are famously bright green — safe to eat but off-putting to the uninitiated.
creatures.behavior: Lives at the surface in loose schools. Leaps from the water when alarmed. Occasional injuring boats and swimmers during frantic escapes.
funFacts: Has bright green bones — due to biliverdin pigment, perfectly safe to eat
Can leap out of the water at speed when startled
Lives its entire life within a metre of the sea surface

creatures.spottingTips: Walks slowly across sandy bottoms on modified pectoral fin rays. When spooked, enormous pectoral fins open to reveal brilliant electric-blue inner colouration. Unmistakeable.
creatures.description: The tub gurnard walks the seafloor on modified fin rays and spreads spectacular blue pectoral wings when startled — one of the most visually striking Mediterranean bottom fish.
creatures.behavior: Walks across the seafloor using pectoral rays as legs, which also taste the sediment for buried prey. Pectoral fins flash open to startle predators.
funFacts: Uses modified pectoral rays as sensory 'feet' to taste the sediment for buried prey
When pectoral fins spread, they reveal a brilliant blue-spotted inner surface
Makes grunting sounds using its swim bladder — hence 'gurnard'

creatures.spottingTips: Lies flat and perfectly camouflaged in sand. Look for an oval outline with a distinctive black pectoral spot. Night dives are best.
creatures.description: The common sole is a masterfully camouflaged flatfish that lies buried in sand by day. One of the most prized food fish in Europe.
creatures.behavior: Lies half-buried in sand by day. Active at night, moving in a wave-like undulation. Born symmetrical — one eye migrates to the right side as a juvenile.
funFacts: Born symmetrical — one eye migrates to the right side of the head during metamorphosis
Can change its skin pattern to match any sandy or muddy bottom
The black spot on the pectoral fin is thought to deter predators

creatures.spottingTips: Nearly impossible to spot — blends seamlessly into sandy or muddy bottoms. Look for a wide flat shape with fringed outline. The lure on its head is tiny and often retracted.
creatures.description: The anglerfish lurks motionless on the seafloor, dangling a fleshy lure to attract prey, then engulfs it with a strike lasting just 6 milliseconds.
creatures.behavior: Completely motionless ambush predator. Waves its illicium (lure) to attract prey, then engulfs it with explosive speed. Can swallow prey up to its own size.
funFacts: Can engulf prey almost as large as itself — its stomach expands enormously
Its strike takes just 6 milliseconds — one of the fastest predatory strikes in the sea
Has been found with diving gannets in its stomach

creatures.spottingTips: Enormous shimmering schools above rocky reefs and in open water. Silver body with 3–4 golden-yellow stripes along the flank. Extremely common for snorkellers.
creatures.description: One of the most abundant pelagic schooling fish in the Mediterranean, forming vast silver-and-gold schools above reef walls.
creatures.behavior: Schooling, semi-pelagic. One of the few seabreams that feeds on algae as well as invertebrates. Protogynous hermaphrodite.
funFacts: Can shift its diet from algae to zooplankton depending on availability
Name comes from Greek 'boop' meaning 'ox-eye', for its large round eyes
One of the most numerous fish in the Mediterranean Sea

creatures.spottingTips: Fast-moving schools in open water near reef walls. Silvery torpedo with distinctive oblique dark stripes on the back and a forked tail.
creatures.description: The Atlantic bonito patrols Mediterranean open waters in fast-moving schools — a smaller tuna cousin that can sustain speeds of 80 km/h.
creatures.behavior: Fast-moving pelagic predator. Hunts in schools, herding sardines and anchovies. Makes regular Mediterranean migrations.
funFacts: Can sustain speeds of up to 80 km/h in short bursts
Like tuna, maintains body temperature above ambient water
Pursues prey to the surface, creating feeding frenzies visible from boats

creatures.spottingTips: Males are unmistakeable — brilliant blue and orange with long extended dorsal fin rays. Females are drab brown. Lie flat on sandy bottoms.
creatures.description: The male common dragonet is one of the most brilliantly coloured fish in the Mediterranean, with electric blue and orange markings and spectacular elongated fin rays.
creatures.behavior: Males display vivid colour to attract drab females. Both sexes lie flat on sandy bottoms. Has no scales — skin covered in thick mucus.
funFacts: Females are drab brown — only males have the brilliant blue colouration
Males change colour intensity within seconds during courtship displays
Has no scales — its skin is covered in a thick mucus instead

creatures.spottingTips: Larger than the lesser-spotted catshark with bigger spots and patches. Rests in crevices and under ledges by day. Completely harmless.
creatures.description: The nursehound is the largest catshark in the Mediterranean, distinguished from the lesser-spotted catshark by its larger size and bigger irregular spots.
creatures.behavior: Rests among rocks by day. Nocturnal hunter. Lays large egg cases anchored to gorgonians.
funFacts: The largest catshark in European waters
Its large rectangular egg cases are found anchored to gorgonians and kelp
Despite its size, is completely harmless to divers

creatures.spottingTips: Swims close to the seafloor in sandy or rocky areas. Uniform grey above, white below, no markings. Moves with a slow, elegant undulation. Harmless and shy.
creatures.description: The common smooth-hound cruises above sandy bottoms crushing crabs and mollusks with its flat, pavement-like teeth. Viviparous — gives birth to live pups.
creatures.behavior: Hunts crustaceans on sandy bottoms. Gives birth to live young (up to 15 pups). Shy and avoids divers.
funFacts: Has flat, pavement-like teeth designed to crush crustacean shells
Viviparous — gives birth to up to 15 live pups
Completely harmless to humans — no sharp biting teeth

creatures.spottingTips: Extremely common in shallow rocky areas. Cannot retract its long tentacles — they remain spread even at low tide. Tentacle tips are bright purple. Mild sting.
creatures.description: The snakelocks anemone harbours photosynthetic algae in its tissues, giving it a green colour. Its tentacles cannot retract and remain permanently extended.
creatures.behavior: Cannot retract its tentacles. Mildly stings prey. Can reproduce by splitting itself in half (fission). Hosts symbiotic photosynthetic algae.
creatures.diet: Small crustaceans, fish, plankton; supplemented by photosynthesis
funFacts: Unlike most anemones, it cannot retract its tentacles — they are always visible
Green colour comes from symbiotic photosynthetic algae in its tissues
Can reproduce by literally tearing itself in half

creatures.spottingTips: Larger than the purple urchin with distinctive white-tipped spines on a violet-blue body. Often sits openly on rocky reef surfaces.
creatures.description: The violet sea urchin is the most handsome urchin in the Mediterranean — its deep violet body is crowned with white-tipped spines unique among Mediterranean urchins.
creatures.behavior: Grazes on algae and encrusting organisms on rocky surfaces. Larger and less gregarious than the purple sea urchin.
funFacts: White-tipped spines are diagnostic — no other Mediterranean urchin has this pattern
Among the largest sea urchins in European waters
Its symmetrical test is collected as a natural ornament

creatures.spottingTips: Found on sandy bottoms, partially buried or moving slowly. Vivid orange-red colour with a comb-like fringe of marginal plates makes it unmistakeable against pale sand.
creatures.description: One of the largest and most striking starfish in the Mediterranean, lying on sandy bottoms to ambush bivalves and sea urchins.
creatures.behavior: Hunts by pressing flat over bivalves and pulling the shell apart. Partially buries itself in sand. Can swallow prey whole by extruding its stomach.
creatures.diet: Bivalves, gastropods, sea urchins, sea cucumbers
funFacts: Can swallow sea urchins whole — spines and all
Has no suckers on its tube feet — uses them like legs to walk over sand
The marginal comb plates along its arms give it its common name

creatures.spottingTips: Found on rocky walls and cave ceilings below 15m. Distinctive very long black spines (up to 30cm) with white banding. Hides in crevices by day.
creatures.description: The long-spined sea urchin has black spines up to 30cm long — the most impressive urchin in the Mediterranean. Strictly protected throughout the EU.
creatures.behavior: Nocturnal. Shelters in rocky crevices by day. Very long spines provide protection and trap detritus as food.
funFacts: Spines can reach 30cm — far longer than those of any other Mediterranean urchin
Strictly protected throughout the EU and Mediterranean
Spines are venomous and can penetrate wetsuits

creatures.spottingTips: Large red-and-yellow fan colonies on rocky walls below 20m, always perpendicular to current. Home to gobies, brittlestars, and nudibranchs.
creatures.description: The iconic red-and-yellow gorgonian creates the defining scenery of deep Mediterranean rocky walls. A single colony can be over a century old, but mass die-offs during marine heatwaves are increasing.
creatures.behavior: Sessile filter feeder. Fan spread perpendicular to current. Extremely sensitive to warming: large-scale die-offs during marine heat waves since 1999.
funFacts: Mass mortality during marine heat waves has killed over 90% of colonies at some sites
A single large colony can be 100+ years old
Home to the nudibranch Tritonia hombergi which perfectly matches its colouration

creatures.spottingTips: The smallest common Diplodus seabream. Identified by a single black ring around the tail base. Often seen in very shallow posidonia meadows and harbour areas.
creatures.description: The annular seabream is the most inshore of all Mediterranean seabreams, happily living in harbours, lagoons, and shallow posidonia. Named for the distinctive black ring at its tail base.
creatures.behavior: Tolerates brackish and low-oxygen water better than other seabreams. Juveniles use very shallow nursery habitats. Forms mixed schools with other small Diplodus species.
funFacts: The most pollution-tolerant of all Mediterranean seabreams — thrives in harbours
Named for the single black ring ('annularis' = ring) at the base of its tail
Juveniles are found in water as shallow as 20cm

creatures.spottingTips: Forms large hyperactive schools just below the surface near rocky coastlines. The black saddle-shaped patch on its tail base is diagnostic. Very commonly seen while snorkelling.
creatures.description: The saddled seabream forms some of the most lively surface schools visible while snorkelling — constantly moving, silvery bodies flashing in sunlit water.
creatures.behavior: Forms large surface schools near rocky coastlines. Omnivorous. Schooling behaviour is spectacular near cliffs and rocky walls.
funFacts: Named for the distinctive black saddle mark at the base of its tail
Schools near the surface are one of the most common snorkelling spectacles in the Mediterranean
Simultaneous hermaphrodite — both male and female at the same time

creatures.spottingTips: Rosy-pink body with a small blue spot above the pectoral fin. Often seen near sandy or muddy bottoms, moving in small groups.
creatures.description: The common pandora is a beautiful rose-red seabream easily identified by the small bright blue spot above its pectoral fin base.
creatures.behavior: Feeds on soft-bottom invertebrates. Protogynous hermaphrodite. Moves to deeper water in winter.
funFacts: Has a diagnostic small bright blue spot just above the pectoral fin
Named after Pandora from Greek mythology
Starts life as female — some individuals become male as they grow larger

creatures.spottingTips: Extremely cryptic — hides in mud, crevices, or under rocks. More likely seen at night. Yellow-brown colouration in coastal areas. One of the most mysterious fish in Europe.
creatures.description: The European eel has one of the most extraordinary life cycles of any animal — born in the Sargasso Sea, it migrates thousands of kilometres to live in Mediterranean coasts, then returns to die.
creatures.behavior: Nocturnal. Lives in fresh and brackish water for 5–20 years, then transforms silver and migrates across the Atlantic to spawn in the Sargasso Sea, where it dies.
funFacts: Nobody has ever observed European eels spawning — it remains a mystery of science
Migrates over 6,000km to the Sargasso Sea to spawn, then dies
Critically endangered — populations have declined over 90% since the 1980s

creatures.spottingTips: One of the largest Mediterranean wrasses. Males are spectacularly coloured in green, blue, and orange. Often seen cruising posidonia meadows and shallow rocky reefs.
creatures.description: The peacock wrasse is the most colourful of the Mediterranean's Symphodus wrasses. Males build nests of seagrass and algae and guard the eggs aggressively.
creatures.behavior: Males build elaborate seagrass nests and attract multiple females. They guard eggs vigorously, fanning them with their fins to oxygenate them.
funFacts: Males build elaborate nests from algae and seagrass to attract females
The largest of the Symphodus wrasses in the Mediterranean
Males are much more brightly coloured than females

creatures.spottingTips: Recognisable by its elongated body and large scales. Variable green-to-brown colouration — males greener, females more brownish. Moves slowly through posidonia.
creatures.description: The green wrasse slowly cruises posidonia meadows and rocky reefs, changing from brown (female) to vivid green (male) over its lifetime.
creatures.behavior: Protogynous hermaphrodite. Builds a nest of seagrass for spawning. Active by day; buries in sand or posidonia at night.
funFacts: Females change into males — and turn green in the process
Buries itself in sand or seagrass at night to sleep
Has distinctive thick lips and large individual scales

creatures.spottingTips: Buries head-first in sand with only eyes and black dorsal fin spines visible. Responsible for the most common venomous fish injuries in the Mediterranean. Shuffle feet when wading.
creatures.description: The greater weever is the most venomous fish in the Mediterranean — buried in sand with only its black venomous dorsal spines exposed, the leading cause of beach injuries.
creatures.behavior: Buries in sand leaving only eyes and black dorsal spines visible. Ambushes prey. Injects venom through dorsal and opercular spines when stepped on.
funFacts: The most venomous fish in the Mediterranean — responsible for thousands of beach injuries per year
Immersion in hot water (as hot as bearable) breaks down the protein-based venom
Shuffling feet along sandy beaches prevents stepping directly on buried weevers

creatures.spottingTips: Forms spectacular clouds of orange-red fish around deep rocky walls and gorgonian fields below 20m. Males have a long third dorsal spine. Among the most photographed fish in the Mediterranean.
creatures.description: The swallowtail sea perch creates dazzling orange clouds around gorgonian-covered walls in deeper Mediterranean waters — one of the most photographed subjects by underwater photographers.
creatures.behavior: Lives in harems overseen by one dominant male. If the male dies, the dominant female sex-changes to replace him. Feeds on zooplankton in mid-water.
funFacts: Lives in harems — the dominant female sex-changes to male if the male disappears
Males develop a spectacular elongated third dorsal fin ray
Forms the most densely photographed underwater aggregations in the Mediterranean

creatures.spottingTips: Brilliant red groups in dark crevices and cave entrances. Emerges at night to feed. Easy to spot on night dives near cave openings — large eyes glow in torch light.
creatures.description: The Mediterranean cardinalfish glows red in cave entrances under ledges. Nocturnal hunter that shelters communally by day; the male incubates eggs in his mouth.
creatures.behavior: Shelters in groups in dark crevices by day. Mouth-brooder — the male carries the egg mass in his mouth for about a month without eating.
funFacts: The male carries the entire egg mass in his mouth for up to a month
Red colouration appears nearly black at depth — invisible to predators
Groups of 5–20 huddle together in cave entrances by day

creatures.spottingTips: Redder and with a steeper head profile than the striped red mullet. Prefers soft muddy and sandy bottoms. Look for small groups probing sediment with their barbels.
creatures.description: The red mullet is redder and deeper-living than the striped red mullet — one of the most prized table fish of the ancient Mediterranean, fetching enormous prices at Roman banquets.
creatures.behavior: Uses twin chin barbels to detect and uncover buried invertebrates in soft sediments.
funFacts: Ancient Romans paid astronomical prices for large red mullets as a status symbol
Can flush bright red and white when excited or dying
Chin barbels withdraw into grooves when not in use

creatures.spottingTips: Large powerful predators around underwater pinnacles and drop-offs. A distinctive amber-yellow band runs from snout through eye to tail. Often curious about divers.
creatures.description: The greater amberjack is the largest jack in the Mediterranean — a powerful predator that patrols underwater pinnacles and cliff edges, often approaching divers boldly.
creatures.behavior: Semi-pelagic, found around seamounts and rocky drop-offs. Hunts in small groups. Highly prized game fish known for powerful runs.
funFacts: A golden-amber stripe runs from eye to tail, giving the species its common name
One of the most powerful game fish in the Mediterranean
Often approaches divers curiously around underwater pinnacles

creatures.spottingTips: Occasionally seen from boats basking at the surface with dorsal fin and bill visible. Extremely rare to encounter underwater. The Strait of Messina is a famous swordfish hotspot.
creatures.description: One of the fastest and most formidable predators in the Mediterranean, reaching 90 km/h. Its flat bill slashes through schools of fish to stun them before eating.
creatures.behavior: Feeds at depth at night, surfaces to warm by day. Solitary. The Strait of Messina has been a traditional fishing ground for centuries.
funFacts: Can reach speeds of up to 90 km/h — one of the fastest fish in the ocean
Has a specialised organ behind the eye that heats the brain to improve hunting
Its bill slashes through fish schools, stunning prey before eating

creatures.spottingTips: Deep-water species rarely seen by recreational divers. Silver-grey body with large mouth and two dorsal fins. More common below 200m on soft bottoms.
creatures.description: The European hake is the most commercially important fish in the Mediterranean, performing nightly vertical migrations from deep water to the surface to hunt.
creatures.behavior: Nightly vertical migrations from 600m+ by day to the surface at night. Juveniles live shallower than adults.
funFacts: Migrates vertically each night — from 600m deep to the surface — following its prey
The most commercially fished species in the Mediterranean
Has two dorsal fins and a distinctive black mouth lining

creatures.spottingTips: Smaller and shallower than the large scorpionfish. Found right in the intertidal zone and rock pools. Sits motionless on rocks. Venomous spines — never touch.
creatures.description: The black scorpionfish is found shallower than the large scorpionfish — right into rock pools — equally well camouflaged and equally venomous, the most commonly encountered scorpionfish by snorkellers.
creatures.behavior: Completely stationary ambush predator in shallower water than its large relative. Can be encountered in rock pools. Sheds skin periodically to remove fouling organisms.
funFacts: Found in rock pools — the most accessible venomous fish in the Mediterranean
Smaller than the large scorpionfish but equally cryptic and equally venomous
The most commonly encountered scorpionfish by snorkellers and swimmers

creatures.spottingTips: Females are unmistakeable: dark grey body with a vivid red-orange tail. Males are duller grey-green. Look for the beak-like fused teeth used to scrape rock surfaces.
creatures.description: The Mediterranean parrotfish is a rare tropical newcomer expanding northward with warming seas. Females are spectacularly coloured with a crimson tail; males are camouflage grey-green.
creatures.behavior: Scrapes algae from rocky surfaces with beak-like fused teeth. Excretes the rock as white sand. Range is expanding northward along Iberian and North African coasts.
creatures.diet: Algae scraped from rock; coralline algae
funFacts: Its fused beak-like teeth can bite chunks off solid rock
Expanding its Mediterranean range northward as the sea warms
One of very few Mediterranean fish that actually produces sand by grinding rock

creatures.spottingTips: Fast, solitary predator seen cruising rocky drop-offs and pinnacles. Silvery body with deeply forked tail. A bold fish that may circle divers. Prized game fish.
creatures.description: The leerfish is a large, powerful solitary predator of Mediterranean rocky coastlines — a fast hunter that ambushes mullet and other fish near the surface.
creatures.behavior: Solitary apex predator. Herds prey against rocky cliff faces or the surface before striking. Highly prized by sport fishermen.
funFacts: One of the fastest accelerating predators in the Mediterranean
Known for herding mullet against rocky cliff faces before striking
Can grow to 2 metres and over 50kg

creatures.spottingTips: Moves slowly across reef surfaces. White bristles along each side look fluffy — NEVER touch. Bristles break off in skin on contact, causing intense burning irritation lasting hours.
creatures.description: The bearded fireworm is a slow-moving polychaete worm covered in white glass-like bristles that break off in skin, causing intense burning pain — hence its name.
creatures.behavior: Grazes on coral, anemones, and gorgonians. White bristles are hollow and contain venom that causes intense contact dermatitis lasting hours.
funFacts: White bristles are hollow glass-like chaetae that shatter on contact and deliver venom
Predatory on slow-moving reef invertebrates including gorgonians and anemones
Originally from the Caribbean — now an expanding invasive species in parts of the Mediterranean

creatures.spottingTips: Lives in a leathery tube in sediment. When undisturbed, spreads a stunning spiral fan of banded purple and white radioles. Retracts instantly when approached — move very slowly.
creatures.description: The peacock worm spreads a beautiful banded fan of feathery radioles when feeding — one of the most elegant sights on Mediterranean sandy and rocky bottoms.
creatures.behavior: Filter feeder. Extends radioles into the current to capture plankton. Retracts instantly into its tube when threatened. Radioles also function as gills.
funFacts: Can retract its entire crown into its tube in a fraction of a second
The banded radioles act simultaneously as gills and feeding apparatus
Builds its tube from secreted mucus mixed with sediment and shell fragments

creatures.spottingTips: Nearly transparent with fine brown banding visible through the shell. Found in rock pools and shallow rocky areas. Visible in crevices under torch light.
creatures.description: The common prawn is the familiar prawn of Mediterranean rock pools — nearly transparent but for delicate brown banding. The species sold as 'fresh prawns' at Mediterranean fish markets.
creatures.behavior: Uses notched rostrum to deter predators. Scavenges and grazes. More active at night.
funFacts: Completely transparent — internal organs are visible through its shell
The rostrum (pointed nose) is serrated — hence 'serratus'
The most commonly eaten shrimp in traditional Mediterranean coastal cuisine

creatures.spottingTips: Hides under rocky ledges with only claws visible. Brilliant red body with electric-blue transverse lines and spines. Emerges to feed at night.
creatures.description: The spiny squat lobster is one of the most strikingly coloured crustaceans in the Mediterranean — vivid red with electric-blue lines — hiding under rocky ledges.
creatures.behavior: Hides in crevices by day. Nocturnal forager. Curls tail under body (squat habit). Aggressive claw displays when threatened.
funFacts: Electric-blue lines on red body make it one of the most striking Mediterranean crustaceans
Technically a crab relative despite the lobster-like appearance
The folded tail distinguishes squat lobsters from true lobsters

creatures.spottingTips: Extremely common on every Mediterranean rocky shore. Scuttles sideways very rapidly when disturbed. Dark green-brown marble pattern on a flat square carapace. Found in the splash zone.
creatures.description: The marbled crab is the most abundant intertidal crab in the entire Mediterranean — found on every rocky shore from Morocco to Lebanon. Familiar to anyone who has explored rock pools.
creatures.behavior: Lives in the intertidal and splash zone. Extremely fast runner. Omnivorous scavenger. Aggressively defends crevice refuges. Can survive hours out of water.
funFacts: The most abundant crab on Mediterranean rocky shores — billions exist across the basin
Despite its tiny size, it is aggressive and will pinch fingers hard
Can survive for hours out of water in the splash zone

creatures.spottingTips: Found on every exposed rocky surface in the intertidal zone. Conical ribbed shell clamped tightly to rock. Look for star-shaped feeding tracks of cleared algae around each limpet.
creatures.description: The Mediterranean limpet is one of the most abundant intertidal animals in the Mediterranean, grazing a territory of bare rock around its precisely returned home scar.
creatures.behavior: Grazes algae at night, returns exactly to its home scar by day. The muscular foot provides extraordinary suction resisting wave forces of 50kg/cm².
funFacts: Returns to exactly the same spot on the rock — its 'home scar' — every single day
Its foot suction can withstand wave impact forces equivalent to 50kg per cm²
Clears a grazing territory visible as a pale ring of bare rock around each limpet

creatures.spottingTips: One of the largest and most beautiful snails in the Mediterranean. Enormous spiral shell with orange and white markings. Rare — protected by EU law. Do not collect.
creatures.description: The triton's trumpet is the largest gastropod in the Mediterranean. It hunts starfish and echinoderms, and its beautiful shell has been used as a ceremonial horn since antiquity.
creatures.behavior: Nocturnal predator. Preys on starfish and sea urchins. Shell used as a war trumpet and ritual horn in ancient Mediterranean cultures.
funFacts: Its shell has been used as a ritual horn across the Mediterranean since the Bronze Age
One of the few predators that can attack and eat crown-of-thorns starfish
Strictly protected — illegal to collect throughout the EU

creatures.spottingTips: Shorter snout than the long-snouted seahorse. Found anchored to posidonia or algae in shallow water. Extremely cryptic — look for the characteristic curled tail gripping seagrass stems.
creatures.description: The short-snouted seahorse is the second of two seahorse species in the Mediterranean — smaller and with a shorter snout than H. guttulatus. Equally cryptic and equally remarkable.
creatures.behavior: Monogamous pairs perform daily greeting rituals. Males carry and birth young from a brood pouch. Anchors to posidonia with its prehensile tail.
funFacts: Shorter snout distinguishes it from the long-snouted seahorse
The father carries the pregnancy and gives birth to the young
Pairs perform a daily greeting dance to reinforce their bond

creatures.spottingTips: Common on sandy and muddy bottoms near estuaries and seagrass. Males darken dramatically during breeding season. Rests motionless on the substrate.
creatures.description: The black goby is one of the most common gobies in the Mediterranean. It inhabits shallow coastal waters, lagoons, and estuaries, often on soft sediments. Males guard and fan eggs deposited in empty shells or crevices.
creatures.behavior: Bottom-dweller that perches on substrate. Males are territorial during breeding and guard the nest aggressively.
funFacts: Males can change colour dramatically when breeding
Uses fused pelvic fins as a suction cup to anchor to rocks
One of the most studied gobies in European coastal ecology

creatures.spottingTips: Peer into rocky crevices and look for their distinctive branched head tentacles. They are curious and will often look back at divers.
creatures.description: The tompot blenny is a charismatic, inquisitive fish of rocky Mediterranean coasts. It sports elaborate branched tentacles above its eyes and is known for its expressive face. A favourite photographic subject.
creatures.behavior: Territorial and curious. Guards nest in rocky crevices where males tend the eggs. Will poke its head out to investigate divers.
funFacts: Named 'tompot' from old English dialect for a rounded pot
Its head tentacles (cirri) are unique to each individual
Males guard and fan the egg mass until hatching

creatures.spottingTips: Found in the intertidal zone — the splash zone on rocky shores. Look in tiny pools and crevices just above the waterline at low tide.
creatures.description: The sphinx blenny lives in the splash zone just above the sea surface — one of the most extreme marine microhabitats. It can breathe air and tolerate desiccation for short periods.
creatures.behavior: Semi-terrestrial. Returns to crevices to keep moist. Can move on land using pectoral fins.
creatures.diet: Algae, small invertebrates in the intertidal zone
funFacts: Lives above the waterline in the splash zone
Can breathe air through its skin when out of water
Named for its habit of resting with its head raised sphinx-like

creatures.spottingTips: Colourful wrasse found around rocky reefs and posidonia. Males are more brightly coloured. Look for the dark spot at the base of the tail.
creatures.description: The corkwing wrasse is a small, colourful wrasse found throughout the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic. It is one of several wrasse species that act as cleaner fish, picking parasites from larger species.
creatures.behavior: Active, curious, often seen cleaning other fish. Males build nests of algae in which females lay eggs.
creatures.diet: Small invertebrates, parasites picked from other fish
funFacts: Acts as a cleaner fish removing ectoparasites from other species
Males construct elaborate seaweed nests
Shows strong sexual dichromatism — males are more colourful

creatures.spottingTips: Common on rocky reefs. Adults are uniformly brownish; juveniles have an orange stripe. They sleep wedged in rock crevices at night.
creatures.description: The brown wrasse is one of the larger wrasse in the Mediterranean. Like many wrasses it is a protogynous hermaphrodite — females can transform into males later in life.
creatures.behavior: Solitary forager. Sleeps in crevices at night. Sex-changing species.
funFacts: Females can change sex to become functional males
Has powerful pharyngeal jaws to crush sea urchins
Sleeps wedged in rocky crevices at night

creatures.spottingTips: Lies flat on sandy or muddy bottoms, almost perfectly camouflaged. The distinctive bright orange-red spots on the dorsal surface are the giveaway.
