creatures.description: The European plaice is a classic flatfish, flattened sideways with both eyes on the right side of the body. It is one of the most commercially important flatfish in Europe and an occasional visitor to Mediterranean waters.
creatures.behavior: Lies motionless on the seafloor, camouflaged against sediment. Migrates to shallower water in spring.
funFacts: Born with eyes on both sides — one migrates during larval development
The bright orange spots make it unique among flatfish
Can change skin colour to match the substrate

creatures.spottingTips: Large flatfish on sandy or gravelly bottoms. Eyes on the left side (sinistral). Covered in small tubercles rather than scales. Master of camouflage.
creatures.description: The turbot is one of the largest flatfish in the Mediterranean and northeastern Atlantic. Unlike most flatfish, both eyes are on the left side. It is a prized food fish and also farmed in aquaculture.
creatures.behavior: Ambush predator lying concealed on the seabed. Actively hunts fish at night.
funFacts: Eyes are on the LEFT side — opposite of most flatfish
Can perfectly mimic the colour and texture of its substrate
One of the most expensive seafood fish in European markets

creatures.spottingTips: Powerful, fast-swimming seabream. Look in deeper rocky areas. Often seen alone or in small groups patrolling reef edges. Canine-like teeth visible at close range.
creatures.description: The common dentex is the largest and most predatory of the Mediterranean seabreams. Its powerful build and canine teeth reflect its role as an active predator rather than a grazer. Highly prized by spearfishers.
creatures.behavior: Active, fast swimmer. Hunts other fish and cephalopods. Adults are largely solitary.
funFacts: One of the few seabreams that is a true fish-eater (piscivore)
Can reach weights of over 10 kg
Changes colour — adults are blue-grey; juveniles have dark spots

creatures.spottingTips: Unmistakable: golden horizontal stripes along the body. Swims in large dense schools over posidonia and rocky reefs. One of the easiest Mediterranean fish to identify.
creatures.description: The salema porgy is a schooling seabream easily recognised by its golden horizontal stripes. It is predominantly herbivorous and grazes on algae and posidonia. It has caused rare cases of ichthyosarcotoxism (fish-borne hallucinations) when consumed.
creatures.behavior: Schools tightly, often in hundreds. Grazes on algae and seagrass.
funFacts: Eating the head has reportedly caused hallucinations in rare documented cases
Golden stripes make it one of the most identifiable Mediterranean fish
Juveniles are found closer to the surface than adults

creatures.spottingTips: Distinctive yellow/gold blotches on a brown body. Found on rocky reefs and around caves. Tend to be solitary and wary of divers.
creatures.description: The goldblotch grouper is a large grouper found in the eastern Mediterranean. Its most distinctive feature is the yellow-orange blotches scattered across its brownish body. Like other groupers, it is a protogynous hermaphrodite.
creatures.behavior: Solitary ambush predator. Rests in caves and overhangs during the day.
funFacts: All goldblotch groupers are born female; large ones transform into males
Eastern Mediterranean endemic grouper species
Can change colour intensity rapidly

creatures.spottingTips: Unmistakable: long, slender fish with an extended snout and a whip-like tail filament. Often hovering horizontally near the surface or over reefs. A Lessepsian invasive species.
creatures.description: The bluespotted cornetfish is a Lessepsian migrant that has become established throughout the eastern Mediterranean. Its elongated body and tubular snout are completely distinctive.
creatures.behavior: Stalks prey slowly, using its long snout to suck in small fish. Often seen alone.
funFacts: Entered the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal (Lessepsian migration)
The filamentous tail tip may help disrupt its outline to prey
One of the most distinctive fish shapes in the Mediterranean

creatures.spottingTips: Dramatically striped red/white. Invasive in the eastern Mediterranean. Floats motionlessly near rocky overhangs or in caves. Do not touch — all spines are venomous.
creatures.description: The devil firefish is a highly venomous Lessepsian invader now common throughout the eastern Mediterranean. Its spectacular red-and-white striped pattern warns of its defensive venomous spines. It has had severe ecological impacts on native fish communities.
creatures.behavior: Slow ambush predator. Uses its pectoral fins to herd prey. Floats motionlessly for long periods.
funFacts: Venom is delivered by 13 dorsal, 2 pelvic, and 3 anal spines
A Lessepsian migrant — invaded the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal
Has dramatically reduced native small-fish populations in the eastern Mediterranean

creatures.spottingTips: Schools of drab grey-brown fish often seen grazing on algae. Invasive in the eastern Mediterranean. Handle with caution — dorsal and pelvic fin spines are venomous.
creatures.description: The dusky spinefoot is a Lessepsian migrant herbivore now very common in the eastern Mediterranean. In schools, it is capable of stripping large areas of algae from rocky reefs, dramatically altering native ecosystems.
creatures.behavior: Schools, grazes on algae voraciously. Has contributed to widespread 'tropicalisation' of eastern Mediterranean reefs.
funFacts: Has transformed entire rocky habitats in the eastern Mediterranean through overgrazing
Schools can denude a rocky reef of all algae — called 'tropicalisation'
Venomous spines despite its herbivorous diet

creatures.spottingTips: Lies buried in sand by day. Mottled brown pattern. Round, almost circular disc body. Do not touch — can deliver an electric shock of up to 200 volts.
creatures.description: The marbled electric ray can produce powerful electric discharges of up to 200 volts using paired electric organs in its disc. It lies buried in sand or mud by day, ambushing prey at night.
creatures.behavior: Buries in sand by day. Ambushes fish at night using an electric shock to stun them.
funFacts: Can deliver a shock of 200 volts to stun prey or defend itself
The ancient Romans used electric rays to treat headaches and gout
Gives birth to live young (viviparous)

creatures.spottingTips: Slender grey shark with white spots along the flanks and a sharp spine in front of each dorsal fin. Now rare in the Mediterranean due to overfishing.
creatures.description: The spiny dogfish has been fished to near-collapse in the Mediterranean. Despite its small size, it has one of the longest gestation periods of any vertebrate — up to 24 months. A spine in front of each dorsal fin can inject mild venom.
creatures.behavior: Schools, often segregated by sex. Migrates seasonally.
funFacts: Gestation lasts up to 24 months — among the longest of any vertebrate
The dorsal spines carry mild venom glands
Critically Endangered in the Mediterranean due to overfishing

creatures.spottingTips: Occasionally ascends to shallower depths at night. Identified by six gill slits (all other Mediterranean sharks have five). A large, ancient-looking shark.
creatures.description: The bluntnose sixgill shark is one of the oldest shark lineages — its basic body plan has barely changed in 200 million years. It normally lives in deep water but occasionally visits shallow reefs at night.
creatures.behavior: Deep-water predator and scavenger. Ascends at night. Generally slow-moving.
funFacts: Its lineage is 200 million years old — predates the dinosaurs
Has six gill slits instead of the usual five
One of the largest existing species of shark

creatures.spottingTips: A whitish nudibranch covered with rounded tubercles. Found on encrusting sponges which it feeds on. Check under rocks and on sponge-covered walls.
creatures.description: The warty doris is one of the common nudibranchs (shell-less sea slugs) in the Mediterranean. Its body is covered in rounded protuberances that give it a warty texture, providing camouflage against encrusting organisms.
creatures.behavior: Slow-moving grazer on sponges. Nocturnal. Deposits eggs in coiled ribbons on rocks.
funFacts: The warts incorporate chemicals from its sponge diet to deter predators
Each doris species specialises on one or few sponge species
Can regenerate body parts if injured

creatures.spottingTips: Vivid purple-violet cerata (projections) along the back. Found on hydroid colonies which it feeds on. Check rocky walls and under ledges.
creatures.description: The purple flabellina is one of the most beautiful and recognisable nudibranchs in the Mediterranean. Its intense purple colour comes from the Eudendrium hydroids it feeds on. Tiny but strikingly vivid.
creatures.behavior: Feeds exclusively on specific hydroid species, whose stinging cells it sequesters into its cerata for defence.
funFacts: Steals stinging cells (nematocysts) from its prey and uses them for defence
Colour intensity reflects the pigments in its hydroid diet
One of the most photographed nudibranchs in the Mediterranean

creatures.spottingTips: Reddish-brown with conspicuous white spots along its very long, slender arms. Arms are notably longer relative to body than the common octopus. Nocturnal and shy.
creatures.description: The white-spotted octopus is recognised by its distinctively long arms and the white spots scattered along them. It is smaller and shyer than the common octopus, and generally more nocturnal.
creatures.behavior: Strictly nocturnal. Hides in crevices by day. More slender and fast-moving than Octopus vulgaris.
funFacts: Arms can be 5 times longer than the body
White spots are retained even when changing colour
More venomous bite than the common octopus

creatures.spottingTips: Distinguished by its variable arm number (usually 7-12). Mottled orange, brown and purple. Found on rocky reefs and in shallow water.
creatures.description: The spiny starfish is unusual among sea stars in having a variable number of arms, typically 7-12 rather than the usual five. It is a common sight on Mediterranean rocky reefs and can reproduce asexually by splitting.
creatures.behavior: Forages actively on rocky reefs. Can reproduce asexually by autotomy (splitting).
funFacts: Has 7-12 arms rather than the standard five of most sea stars
Can reproduce asexually by splitting its body in two
Each arm fragment can regenerate a complete animal

creatures.spottingTips: Five arms covered with prominent spiny tubercles arranged in rows. Greyish-green to purple. One of the larger Mediterranean starfish. Found on rocky reefs.
creatures.description: The glacial spiny starfish is one of the largest sea stars in the Mediterranean. Its five arms are covered with rows of prominent spiny tubercles. It is a significant predator of mussels, oysters, and sea urchins.
creatures.behavior: Active predator. Climbs mussel beds and pries open bivalves by sustained pulling. Can detect prey from a distance.
funFacts: Can exert enough force to open a mussel by sustained pulling
Has rows of spiny tubercles unique among Mediterranean starfish
Regenerates amputated arms over several months

creatures.spottingTips: Larger than the common urchins, with shorter, stouter spines. Whitish to pale pink. Found on rocky reefs from moderate to deep water.
creatures.description: Echinus melo is one of the larger sea urchins found in deeper Mediterranean waters. Its short, stout spines and large test (shell) distinguish it from the more common Paracentrotus lividus of shallow water.
creatures.behavior: Moves slowly across rocky surfaces, grazing on encrusting organisms.
funFacts: One of the largest sea urchins in the Mediterranean
Its round test (shell) has been used as a decorative object
Can live for decades

creatures.spottingTips: Vivid yellow clusters of tiny polyps coating rocky walls and overhangs. Often found alongside orange cup corals. The yellow colour is unmistakable in the blue-green underwater light.
creatures.description: Parazoanthus axinellae forms dense colonies of bright yellow polyps on rocky walls, cave ceilings, and overhangs throughout the Mediterranean. It is not a true coral but a zoanthid — a colonial anthozoan closely related to anemones.
creatures.behavior: Colonial filter feeder. Polyps extend to feed on plankton; retract when disturbed.
funFacts: The yellow pigment is a zooxanthellae-independent coloration
Often encrusts over the sponge Axinella — the genus name hints at this
Each polyp is an individual animal sharing a common colony skeleton

creatures.spottingTips: The only zooxanthellate (reef-building) coral in the Mediterranean. Forms cushion-shaped colonies with visible polyp tubes. Found in shallow warm waters.
creatures.description: Cladocora caespitosa is the only Mediterranean coral with symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae), making it the closest equivalent to tropical reef-building corals. It forms cushion-shaped colonies and is highly vulnerable to warming seas.
creatures.behavior: Sessile filter feeder. Bleaches (expels symbiotic algae) during heat stress, like tropical corals.
creatures.diet: Zooplankton, dissolved organic matter via symbiotic algae
funFacts: The only zooxanthellate coral in the Mediterranean — unique among European seas
Bleaches during marine heatwaves — a canary for climate change
Colonies can be centuries old

creatures.spottingTips: The largest goby in the Mediterranean. Found in rock pools and very shallow water. Look in tide pools — it is the big fish in the puddle.
creatures.description: The giant goby is the largest goby in the Mediterranean, yet still a modest fish rarely exceeding 27 cm. It inhabits shallow rock pools and the immediate subtidal zone. Despite its name, it is overshadowed by its sheer commonness.
creatures.behavior: Territorial in rock pools. Males guard eggs laid in crevices.
funFacts: Despite the name 'giant', it is still a relatively small fish
The largest goby species in Mediterranean waters
Rock-pool inhabitants recognise individual giant gobies over several months

creatures.spottingTips: Dense silvery schools near the surface in bays, lagoons, and harbours. A silver stripe along the flank. Extremely common and easily seen from piers.
creatures.description: The big-scale sand smelt is one of the most abundant small fish in Mediterranean coastal and estuarine waters. It forms large dense schools near the surface and is a critical prey item for larger predators, seabirds, and humans.
creatures.behavior: Schools densely near the surface. Spawns in shallow water by attaching adhesive eggs to algae and vegetation.
funFacts: One of the most abundant nearshore fish in the entire Mediterranean
Schools are so dense they can be scooped from the water with a net
Known as 'nons' in Catalan cuisine — eaten whole, fried

creatures.spottingTips: Large silvery schools near the surface in harbours, estuaries, and shallow bays. Frequently seen jumping clear of the water. Distinctive broad, flat head.
creatures.description: The flathead mullet is a widely distributed species found worldwide in coastal and brackish waters. In the Mediterranean it is common in harbours, lagoons, and estuaries. It is farmed for its prized roe (bottarga).
creatures.behavior: Schools near the surface. Grazes on bottom sediment and algae. Famous for leaping.
creatures.diet: Algae, organic detritus, biofilm, benthic invertebrates
funFacts: Its roe, pressed and dried, is 'bottarga' — a prized Mediterranean delicacy
Has a muscular gizzard-like stomach to grind sediment
Frequently leaps clear of the water, possibly to avoid predators

creatures.spottingTips: Forms large schools over posidonia and sandy bottoms at moderate depths. Distinguished by a dark blotch on the flank (more prominent in males during breeding). A very common Mediterranean fish.
creatures.description: The blotched picarel is an abundant small fish that forms large schools in the Mediterranean. It is a protogynous hermaphrodite and an important prey species for larger fish. The dark lateral blotch distinguishes it from related species.
creatures.behavior: Schools in large groups. Males excavate nests in sandy bottoms and guard eggs. Protogynous hermaphrodite.
funFacts: Starts life as female and becomes male later
Males excavate nesting pits in sand to attract females
One of the most abundant fish in Mediterranean seagrass meadows

creatures.spottingTips: Unmistakable vertical black and white stripes on the body — like a zebra. Found on rocky reefs. More solitary than other Diplodus species.
creatures.description: The zebra seabream is one of the most strikingly patterned fish in the Mediterranean, with bold vertical black-and-white stripes across its body. It is less common than other seabreams and prefers deeper rocky habitats.
creatures.behavior: Solitary or in small groups. Forages on rocky reefs for invertebrates.
funFacts: The vertical stripes make it instantly recognisable
Named cervinus (deer-like) for its spotted colour pattern at younger stages
Less studied than other Diplodus species due to lower commercial value

creatures.spottingTips: Has a shark-like tail combined with a flat, ray-like flattened front. The pointed triangular snout is distinctive. Found on sandy bottoms, often partially buried.
creatures.description: The common guitarfish is a batoid (skate/ray relative) with an intermediate body form between sharks and rays. Its shark-like tail and flat disc body give it a guitar-like profile. Once common, it is now critically endangered in the Mediterranean.
creatures.behavior: Rests on sandy or muddy bottoms. Swims with undulating body movements like a shark.
funFacts: Combines shark-like tail with ray-like flat body
Critically Endangered in the Mediterranean due to bycatch
Its embryos are enclosed in egg cases that are eventually born live

creatures.spottingTips: The second largest fish in the world. Look for the large dorsal fin and caudal fin cutting the surface. Slow-moving, mouth agape at the surface filtering plankton. Rare but memorable sight.
creatures.description: The basking shark is the world's second largest fish, reaching up to 12 metres. Despite its enormous size it feeds solely on zooplankton filtered through massive gill arches. It occasionally visits the Mediterranean in spring.
creatures.behavior: Filter-feeds at the surface with its huge mouth open. Aggregates where plankton is concentrated.
funFacts: Second largest fish in the world after the whale shark
Filters up to 2,000 tonnes of water per hour through its gill arches
Despite its size, its brain is tiny — about the size of a fist

creatures.spottingTips: Grey dolphin heavily scarred with white scratches from squid bites. Blunt, rounded head — no beak. Often seen porpoising near canyon edges and deep offshore waters.
creatures.description: Risso's dolphin is a deep-water cetacean that feeds almost exclusively on squid. Adults become increasingly pale and scar-covered with age as squid bite them during capture. It prefers deep offshore waters near submarine canyons.
creatures.behavior: Deep diver. Groups of 10–50. Less acrobatic than common dolphins. Scars accumulate throughout life.
funFacts: Adults are almost completely white due to accumulated squid scars
No beak — the blunt head and lack of rostrum make it unique among dolphins
Can dive to over 500 m to hunt squid

creatures.spottingTips: Fastest Mediterranean dolphin. Identified by the distinctive yellow-tan and grey hourglass pattern on the flank. Often bow-rides on boats. Large, exuberant groups.
creatures.description: The short-beaked common dolphin has declined dramatically in the Mediterranean — once highly abundant, it has been reduced primarily by prey depletion and incidental bycatch. Historically it was the most common dolphin in the basin.
creatures.behavior: Highly social, forms schools of hundreds. Bow-rides enthusiastically on vessel wakes. Fast swimmer.
funFacts: The 'common' dolphin is now rare in much of the Mediterranean
Its distinctive hourglass pattern is unique among dolphins
Appears in ancient Greek and Roman art — the archetypal dolphin

creatures.spottingTips: Rarely seen at the surface. Short beak and robust body. Often bears white oval scars. The Mediterranean population uses the Ligurian Sea. Look for the small blowhole visible from a distance.
creatures.description: Cuvier's beaked whale is the deepest-diving air-breathing animal known, capable of dives to nearly 3,000 metres. The Mediterranean population, centred in the Ligurian Sea, is severely threatened by military sonar and ship strikes.
creatures.behavior: Spends little time at the surface. Performs extreme dives lasting over two hours. Extremely shy of boats.
funFacts: Holds the record for deepest dive by a mammal — nearly 3,000 metres
Dives can last over 3 hours
Mediterranean population is classified as Endangered and is among the most at-risk cetaceans in Europe

creatures.spottingTips: Distinguished by its very large first dorsal fin — disproportionately tall compared to other requiem sharks. Stocky build. Found over sandy bottoms in coastal and offshore waters.
creatures.description: The sandbar shark is one of the most abundant large sharks globally but rare in the Mediterranean. It is recognised by its exceptionally large first dorsal fin. A slow-to-mature, long-lived species vulnerable to overfishing.
creatures.behavior: Coastal to pelagic. Females use coastal nursery areas. Generally not aggressive towards humans.
funFacts: Has the largest dorsal fin relative to body size of any requiem shark
One of the most studied sharks in the world due to its abundance elsewhere
Females give birth in coastal nursery areas

creatures.spottingTips: Long, narrow, tightly coiled spiral shell, usually brownish. Found on soft sediment bottoms, often in large aggregations. Empty shells are commonly washed up on beaches.
creatures.description: The tower shell is a slender, elongate gastropod that lives half-buried in sandy or muddy sediments. It is a suspension feeder, gathering food particles from the water with its gill cilia. Empty shells are commonly found on Mediterranean beaches.
creatures.behavior: Lives partially buried in soft sediment. Suspension feeds. Moves very slowly.
creatures.diet: Phytoplankton, detritus filtered from the water
funFacts: The tightly coiled spire can have up to 20 whorls
Empty shells are frequently inhabited by hermit crabs
A common fossil in Mediterranean Pliocene sediments

creatures.spottingTips: Conical shell with brown and white banding. Found under rocks and on rocky surfaces. Do not handle carelessly — although Mediterranean cones are less venomous than tropical relatives, they can still sting.
creatures.description: The Mediterranean cone is the only cone snail native to the Mediterranean. Like all cone snails it can deliver a venomous sting via a harpoon-like tooth, though the Mediterranean species is far less dangerous than its tropical relatives.
creatures.behavior: Nocturnal predator. Uses venom-injecting tooth to paralyse prey.
funFacts: The only cone snail native to the Mediterranean Sea
All cone snails are venomous — the Mediterranean species is milder than tropical cones
Compounds from cone snail venom are being researched for pain medicine

creatures.spottingTips: Flat oval shell with a row of holes along one edge. Clings tightly to rocky surfaces. The interior shell is iridescent mother-of-pearl. Now rare due to overexploitation.
creatures.description: The green ormer is the only abalone (Haliotis) native to the Mediterranean. Its flat, ear-shaped shell has a row of respiratory holes along one edge. The iridescent interior was used in jewellery. Now rare due to overcollection.
creatures.behavior: Nocturnal grazer. Clings powerfully to rock surfaces with its muscular foot. Grazes on coralline and encrusting algae.
funFacts: The only abalone native to the Mediterranean and European coasts
The row of respiratory holes is unique among gastropods
Interior shell is brilliant iridescent mother-of-pearl

creatures.spottingTips: Smaller than the spiny spider crab. Covered in hooked hairs used to attach camouflage material. Often disguises itself with algae and sponge fragments. Rocky and posidonia habitats.
creatures.description: The Mediterranean spider crab (not to be confused with the larger Maja squinado) is a small, well-camouflaged decorator crab that attaches algae, sponges, and other material to its shell. This provides excellent camouflage on rocky and posidonia habitats.
creatures.behavior: Nocturnal. Actively decorates its carapace with environmental material. Moves slowly.
funFacts: Actively selects and attaches camouflage materials to its shell
The hooked hairs (setae) act as Velcro to hold the disguise
Changes its disguise when moved to a new environment

creatures.spottingTips: Reddish-brown crab with very unequal, heavy claws and distinctive red eyes. Found in rock crevices in the intertidal and shallow subtidal zones. Very common and robust.
creatures.description: The warty crab is a common and robust crab of Mediterranean rocky shores. It has exceptionally strong, unequal claws used to crack open molluscs. It inhabits crevices in the intertidal and shallow subtidal zone and is often encountered by snorkellers.
creatures.behavior: Nocturnal. Hides in crevices by day. Uses powerful claws to crush mollusc prey.
funFacts: Its claws are powerful enough to crack open thick-shelled limpets and mussels
The two claws are often markedly different in size
Named 'warty' for the tubercles covering its carapace and claws

creatures.spottingTips: Extremely abundant in rock pools and shallow water. Small hermit crabs carrying borrowed shells. Identifiable by blue-grey and orange striped walking legs. Ubiquitous on Mediterranean rocky shores.
creatures.description: The ringed hermit crab is one of the most abundant small crustaceans on Mediterranean rocky shores. It inhabits empty gastropod shells for protection, exchanging shells as it grows. Large aggregations gather for shell exchanges.
creatures.behavior: Carries a borrowed gastropod shell. Gathers in groups to exchange shells as individuals grow. Omnivorous scavenger.
creatures.diet: Algae, detritus, dead organic matter, small invertebrates
funFacts: Exchanges shells in coordinated groups — individuals swap in sequence
Blue-grey and orange leg stripes make it identifiable from other hermit crab species
Can sometimes be seen in mass gatherings of hundreds near shell piles

creatures.spottingTips: Found in cave entrances and on walls in subdued light. The orange-red and white banded claws are very long relative to the body. Usually found in pairs under overhangs.
creatures.description: The Mediterranean boxer shrimp is the only banded coral shrimp in the Mediterranean. It is found in caves and dark overhangs where it lives in permanent pairs. It acts as a cleaner shrimp, servicing fish that come to its station.
creatures.behavior: Lives in monogamous pairs. Acts as a cleaner station. Nocturnal forager.
creatures.diet: Parasites and dead tissue removed from fish, detritus, small invertebrates
funFacts: The only representative of its tropical family in the Mediterranean
Lives in permanent monogamous pairs for life
The enormously long banded chelipeds (claws) inspired the name 'boxer'

creatures.spottingTips: Flattened anglerfish with a broad head and massive upturned mouth. Black peritoneum (inner body lining). Lies perfectly camouflaged on the seabed. Less common than Lophius piscatorius.
creatures.description: The black-bellied anglerfish is distinguished from the common anglerfish (Lophius piscatorius) by its black inner body cavity. It tends to live in deeper water. Both species use a modified dorsal spine as a lure to attract prey.
creatures.behavior: Lies motionless on the seabed, attracting prey with the lure on its modified first dorsal spine.
funFacts: Named for its black peritoneum — the membrane lining its body cavity
The 'lure' on its head is a modified dorsal spine called the illicium
Can swallow prey almost as large as itself thanks to its expandable stomach

creatures.spottingTips: Branching finger-like purple or blue-grey sponge. Very common on rocky walls and in caves. A characteristic component of Mediterranean rocky reef communities.
creatures.description: Haliclona mediterranea is a common encrusting and branching sponge of Mediterranean rocky habitats. It forms pale violet to grey branching masses or thin encrusting sheets on rocky walls and in caves, and is an important component of hard-substrate communities.
creatures.behavior: Sessile filter feeder. Pumps water through its body to filter food particles.
funFacts: A single sponge can filter hundreds of litres of water per day
Sponges are animals — one of the simplest multicellular animals on Earth
Some compounds isolated from Mediterranean sponges have antimicrobial properties

creatures.spottingTips: Bright orange massive or branching sponge. Distinctive and photogenic. Found on rocky walls and in cave entrances. The orange colour is vivid against the blue water.
creatures.description: Agelas oroides is one of the most conspicuous sponges in the Mediterranean, forming large bright orange or yellow-orange masses on rocky walls and cave entrances. It is a characteristic component of coralligenous and cave communities.
creatures.behavior: Sessile filter feeder. Slow-growing. Long-lived.
funFacts: One of the most vivid and photogenic sponges in the Mediterranean
Produces bromopyrrole alkaloids with potent antimicrobial activity
Can live for decades, growing slowly on rocky walls

creatures.spottingTips: Dense brown-olive seaweed forming turfs on wave-exposed rocky shores in the intertidal zone. Forms distinct horizontal bands on rocks. A bioindicator of water quality.
creatures.description: Cystoseira amentacea is a large brown macroalga that forms dense intertidal forests on wave-exposed rocky shores throughout the Mediterranean. It is a key structuring species and a highly sensitive indicator of water quality.
creatures.behavior: Sessile. Provides habitat and food for many invertebrates. Air vesicles help it stay upright in water.
funFacts: A bioindicator — its absence signals water pollution or physical disturbance
Forms multi-layered 'forests' that provide habitat for hundreds of species
Has declined dramatically in urbanised coastal areas due to pollution

creatures.spottingTips: Fast, aggressive predator. Often seen slashing through schools of smaller fish near the surface. Schools of bluefish are betrayed by frenzied activity at the surface and seabirds diving.
creatures.description: The bluefish is one of the most voracious predators in the Mediterranean, famous for its feeding frenzies where entire schools slash through baitfish. It is a highly prized sport fish and an important commercial species.
creatures.behavior: Schools and actively hunts in coordinated attacks. Known for killing more prey than it eats during feeding frenzies.
funFacts: Will continue biting even after it is full — known for 'wasteful' killing
Sharp teeth can inflict serious wounds if handled carelessly
Migrates seasonally, following schools of prey fish

creatures.spottingTips: Spectacular iridescent blue-green and yellow fish found near floating objects, driftwood, or FADs at the surface. The blunt forehead (especially in males) is distinctive.
creatures.description: The dolphinfish (also called mahi-mahi) is one of the most spectacular pelagic fish in the Mediterranean, displaying vivid blue, green and gold iridescence. Males have a prominent blunt forehead. It is one of the fastest-growing fish in the ocean.
creatures.behavior: Associates with floating objects (logs, debris, FADs). Fast swimmer. Leaps from the water when hooked.
funFacts: One of the fastest-growing fish — reaches full size in under a year
Males (bulls) have a distinctive high, blunt forehead
The vivid colours fade within seconds of death

creatures.spottingTips: Pinkish-red seabream with a characteristic dark spot at the base of the pectoral fin. Found over sandy and mixed bottoms. Common but easily confused with other red/pink seabreams.
creatures.description: The common pandora is a pinkish seabream found throughout the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic. It is a protogynous hermaphrodite, often forming mixed schools with other seabream species. A commercially important species.
creatures.behavior: Schools over sandy and rocky bottoms. Protogynous hermaphrodite (starts as female, becomes male).
funFacts: Named pandora from the Greek — possibly for its variably mottled colouring
A dark blotch at the pectoral fin base is a key identification feature
Starts life as female, transforms to male after several years

creatures.spottingTips: Smaller than Scorpaena scrofa. Look for a distinctive large dark spot on the dorsal fin. Sits motionless on rocky surfaces. All scorpionfish spines are venomous — do not touch.
creatures.description: The small red scorpionfish is one of the most common scorpionfish in the Mediterranean shallows. Like its larger relatives it uses perfect camouflage and a sit-and-wait strategy to ambush prey. Its dorsal spines are venomous.
creatures.behavior: Sits motionless on rocky substrates. Swallows prey whole with a rapid strike.
funFacts: Identified by the large dark blotch on the dorsal fin
Can change colour to match surrounding substrate within days
Venom in the dorsal spines causes intense localised pain

creatures.spottingTips: Small, colourful fish often seen on sandy or posidonia bottoms. Brown and white banding with a dark blotch on the dorsal fin. Often hovers just above the bottom.
creatures.description: The brown comber is one of the smallest and most common combers in the Mediterranean. Like all Serranus species it is a simultaneous hermaphrodite — every individual is male and female at the same time.
creatures.behavior: Solitary. Perches near the bottom. Self-fertilising simultaneous hermaphrodite.
funFacts: Can self-fertilise — every individual is simultaneously male and female
Despite being common, it is easily overlooked due to its small size
Closely related to the larger groupers

creatures.spottingTips: Small goby with a strikingly bright yellow-orange head. Found on rocky walls and cave entrances. Males display intensely during breeding season.
creatures.description: The yellow-headed goby is one of the most attractive Mediterranean gobies. Males develop a brilliant yellow-orange head during the breeding season. It inhabits rocky walls and cave entrances across the western Mediterranean.
creatures.behavior: Males guard eggs deposited in crevices. Territorial. Often seen perched on vertical rock surfaces.
funFacts: The vivid yellow head is a breeding coloration in males
A Mediterranean endemic, found nowhere else in the world
Males court females with lateral display showing off their bright heads

creatures.spottingTips: Males are strikingly blue and orange — among the most vividly coloured Mediterranean fish. Females are orange with dark dorsal blotches. One of the most photogenic reef fish.
creatures.description: The cuckoo wrasse shows extreme sexual dichromatism: females are salmon-orange with black dorsal spots; males are brilliant blue and orange. Like all wrasses, it is a protogynous hermaphrodite — females transform into males.
creatures.behavior: Males actively patrol reef territories. Females less conspicuous. Sex change occurs when dominant male is absent.
funFacts: Males are brilliant blue and orange — one of the most colourful fish in the Mediterranean
Females are orange with dark blotches — same species, completely different appearance
All males were once female

creatures.spottingTips: Pinkish-white fish with a bold yellow stripe from snout to tail. Lessepsian invader now common in the eastern Mediterranean. Uses long chin barbels to probe the sand for food.
creatures.description: The goldband goatfish is a Lessepsian migrant from the Red Sea, now one of the most abundant fish on eastern Mediterranean sandy and rocky bottoms. Its distinctive yellow lateral stripe makes it unmistakable.
creatures.behavior: Probes sandy bottoms with sensitive barbels to find buried invertebrates.
creatures.diet: Small invertebrates buried in sand — worms, crustaceans, molluscs
funFacts: Entered the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal
The chin barbels are chemosensory organs used to detect buried prey
Now outcompetes the native red mullet in some eastern Mediterranean areas

creatures.spottingTips: A large, slug-like animal with rolled ear-like tentacles (rhinophores) that give it the 'hare' appearance. Often found in posidonia and on algae-covered rocks. Releases purple ink when disturbed.
creatures.description: The sea hare is a large shell-less gastropod (opisthobranch) with a soft, mottled brownish body. It has two large rolled tentacles resembling hare ears. When threatened, it releases a cloud of purple-pink ink to confuse predators.
creatures.behavior: Grazes on algae. Releases ink when disturbed. Forms large mating aggregations in spring.
funFacts: Releases a purple-pink ink cloud as a defence mechanism
In spring, dozens can form mating chains where each individual is simultaneously male and female
The ink may also contain toxins derived from red algae in its diet

creatures.spottingTips: Encrusted bivalve with long, ornate spines projecting from its orange-red shell. Cemented to rocky walls. Often encrusted with other organisms. Spectacular when the shell is clean.
creatures.description: The European thorny oyster is among the most ornate bivalves in the Mediterranean. Its shell is covered in long, curved spines and is brilliantly coloured orange-red. It cements itself permanently to rocky surfaces and is often overgrown with other organisms.
creatures.behavior: Sessile. Filter feeds with its mantle extended. Reacts to shadows by snapping shut.
funFacts: The long spines are thought to deter predators and provide attachment points for other organisms
The interior is strikingly purple and white
Has 'eyes' — rows of tiny photoreceptors along the mantle edge to detect approaching shadows

creatures.spottingTips: Smooth, glossy, oval shell that is mottled brown above and pale below. Found under rocks and on sponge-covered surfaces. The living animal covers the shell with its colourful mantle when active.
creatures.description: The Mediterranean cowrie is one of two cowrie species native to the Mediterranean. Its smooth, porcelain-like shell is distinctive. When alive, the mantle tissue extends over the shell, maintaining its glossy surface.
creatures.behavior: Nocturnal. Feeds on colonial tunicates and sponges. Hides under rocks by day.
creatures.diet: Colonial tunicates (sea squirts), sponges, encrusting bryozoans
funFacts: The mantle completely covers and polishes the shell while the animal is alive
One of only two cowrie species in the Mediterranean
Cowrie shells were used as currency in many ancient cultures

creatures.spottingTips: Pale orange lobster-like crustacean that emerges from burrows at night. Found on muddy bottoms at moderate to deep depths. Peek into burrow openings at dusk.
creatures.description: The Norway lobster, known commercially as langoustine or scampi, is a slender pale orange crustacean that lives in burrows in muddy Mediterranean and Atlantic bottoms. It is one of the most commercially valuable crustaceans in European waters.
creatures.behavior: Burrow-dweller. Emerges to feed at night. Males and females have separate burrows.
funFacts: The basis of the famous Italian dish 'scampi' and the Scottish 'langoustine'
Each individual excavates and maintains its own burrow system
Population size can be estimated by counting burrow openings from a submarine

creatures.spottingTips: The largest European crustacean. Deep blue when alive (turns red only when cooked). Hides in rock crevices by day. Look for the large unequal claws. Now rare due to heavy fishing pressure.
creatures.description: The European lobster is the largest crustacean in the Mediterranean and northeastern Atlantic. Unlike the North American lobster, it is deep blue when alive. It is rarely seen due to its nocturnal habits and heavy fishing pressure.
creatures.behavior: Nocturnal. Hides in rock dens by day. The larger claw crushes prey; the smaller claw cuts.
funFacts: Deep royal blue when alive — only turns red when cooked
The two claws are different: one for crushing, one for cutting
Can live for over 50 years and continue growing throughout life

creatures.spottingTips: Distinctive thick, club-shaped primary spines (not the typical needle spines of other urchins). Found on deeper rocky reefs and walls. The spines are encrusted with bryozoans and hydroids.
creatures.description: The club urchin is a primitive sea urchin with thick, club-shaped primary spines that become colonised by bryozoans, sponges, and hydroids. It is found on deeper rocky reefs and walls in the Mediterranean and northeastern Atlantic.
creatures.behavior: Slow-moving. Lives on rocky substrates. Spines host a community of encrusting organisms.
funFacts: The thick spines can host entire communities of small invertebrates
One of the most primitive living echinoid families
The test (shell) has been used in jewellery and as a collectible

creatures.spottingTips: Large, black, cylindrical sea cucumber with rows of yellowish tube feet visible beneath. Very common on rocky and mixed substrates. Named for its ability to expel sticky white threads (Cuvierian tubules) when threatened.
creatures.description: The cotton-spinner is one of the most common sea cucumbers in the Mediterranean. When threatened it expels sticky white threads (Cuvierian tubules) that entangle and repel predators. These threads can later be regenerated.
creatures.behavior: Crawls slowly over hard and soft substrates. Ejects sticky white threads when threatened.
creatures.diet: Organic detritus and sediment, processed through the gut
funFacts: Ejects sticky white 'cotton' threads from its anus to entangle predators
Named cotton-spinner for these defensive threads
Can regenerate the expelled threads within a few weeks

creatures.spottingTips: Brilliant blue oval float with a transparent diagonal sail. Found at the sea surface, sometimes in thousands after onshore winds. Beached individuals are safe to touch but tentacles of fresh ones may irritate skin.
creatures.description: Velella velella is a colonial hydrozoan that lives permanently at the sea surface, driven by wind via its transparent sail. It is not a true jellyfish but a colony of polyps. It turns purple and dries to a silvery skeleton when beached.
creatures.behavior: Passive drifter at the ocean surface. Oriented at 45° to the wind. Tentacles capture small plankton.
funFacts: Not a single animal but a colony of zooids, each specialised for feeding, reproduction, or flotation
Mass strandings of millions can carpet Mediterranean beaches
Turns from brilliant blue to silver-white when dried on the beach

creatures.spottingTips: Very small, nearly transparent box-shaped bell. Difficult to see at sea. More likely to be encountered at night near the surface. Sting is significantly more painful than most Mediterranean jellyfish — avoid contact.
creatures.description: The Mediterranean box jellyfish is the only cubozoan (box jellyfish) in the Mediterranean. While far less dangerous than its tropical relatives, its sting is more painful and persistent than common jellyfish. It is small and nearly invisible in the water.
creatures.behavior: Active swimmer — box jellyfish can swim directionally, unlike true jellyfish. Active at night near the surface.
funFacts: The only box jellyfish in the Mediterranean
Unlike true jellyfish, box jellyfish have eyes with lenses — they can see
Can swim directionally, unlike the passive drift of true jellyfish

creatures.spottingTips: Large, fan-like or encrusting orange-red colonies on rocky walls and cave entrances. Not a true coral but a bryozoan. Very common on Mediterranean rocky reefs. Forms large, fragile colonies.
creatures.description: Ross coral is one of the most characteristic animals of Mediterranean rocky reef communities. Despite its name, it is a bryozoan — a colony of tiny zooids — not a true coral. Its large orange-red fan-shaped colonies are a defining feature of coralligenous habitats.
creatures.behavior: Sessile colonial filter feeder. Zooids extend their lophophores (feeding tentacles) to capture particles.
funFacts: Not a coral — a bryozoan, related to lampshells
Each zooid is the size of a pinhead; the colony contains millions
A key indicator species of healthy coralligenous habitat

creatures.spottingTips: Lobed orange or orange-white soft coral forming rounded or finger-like masses on rocky walls. The polyps are white and visible when extended. Common on shaded walls and cave entrances.
creatures.description: Alcyonium acaule is a soft coral that forms orange, lobed masses on shaded rocky surfaces and cave walls throughout the Mediterranean. When its white polyps are extended it looks furry. It is a key component of coralligenous and cave communities.
creatures.behavior: Sessile colonial filter feeder. Polyps retract when disturbed.
funFacts: The lobed, finger-like shape inspired the English common name 'dead man's fingers'
Related species in the North Atlantic also bears this common name
Soft corals lack the hard calcium carbonate skeleton of true corals

creatures.spottingTips: Narrow seagrass leaves, shorter and narrower than Posidonia. Forms meadows on sandy bottoms, often in shallower or more turbid water than Posidonia. A pioneer species colonising bare sand.
creatures.description: Cymodocea nodosa is a seagrass that forms extensive meadows in shallow Mediterranean waters, particularly in lagoonal and sheltered environments. It is a pioneer species, colonising bare sandy areas, and is less sensitive than Posidonia oceanica.
creatures.behavior: Spreads via rhizomes (underground stems). Forms continuous meadows that stabilise sediment.
creatures.diet: Photosynthesis and root uptake of nutrients
funFacts: A pioneer species that colonises bare sand before Posidonia takes over
Leaves can be mistaken for Posidonia but are narrower and shorter
Provides nursery habitat for many juvenile fish and invertebrates

creatures.spottingTips: Bright green, segmented, calcareous alga with rounded flattened segments joined in chains. Common on rocky and sandy bottoms. The calcified segments turn white when the alga dies.
creatures.description: Halimeda tuna is a calcareous green alga common throughout the Mediterranean. Its rounded, flattened, calcified segments give it a distinctive beaded-chain appearance. When it dies, the white calcified segments accumulate in sediments.
creatures.behavior: Sessile. Reproduces both vegetatively (fragmentation) and sexually.
funFacts: Its calcified segments contribute to carbonate sediment formation
Despite being a plant-like organism, produces chemicals to deter fish grazing
One of the few algae that calcifies — like a coral
